passage.title: The box that changed the world

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few inventions have altered daily life as much as the steel shipping container, and few have received so little attention. It has no engine, no moving parts and no obvious ingenuity. Yet without it, the cheap clothes, electronics and out-of-season fruit that fill the shops of the world would cost far more, and many of the factories that make them would stand in different countries.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the twentieth century, cargo was handled much as it had been for hundreds of years. Goods arrived at the quay in sacks, barrels, crates and bales of every size, and each item was carried into the hold by gangs of dockworkers and stacked by hand. A ship could spend more time tied up in port than at sea. Breakages were frequent, and theft was so routine that dockers joked about being paid twenty dollars a day and all the whisky they could carry home. For many products, the expense of getting on and off the ship was greater than the cost of crossing the ocean.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The man usually credited with changing this was not a shipowner but an American trucking entrepreneur, Malcolm McLean. Waiting for hours at a New Jersey pier in the 1930s while his lorry was unloaded piece by piece, he had wondered why the whole trailer could not simply be lifted on board. Twenty years later he bought a shipping company in order to try. In April 1956 a converted oil tanker, the Ideal X, sailed from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight metal boxes on a specially built deck. When the accounts were done, loading had cost less than sixteen cents a ton, compared with nearly six dollars for loose cargo.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The idea did not spread at once. Early containers came in a confusion of lengths, and a box designed for one company's ships and cranes would not fit another's. It took more than a decade of argument between shipping lines, railway companies and governments before international standards were agreed in the late 1960s. Crucially, McLean chose to release his patent on the corner fittings that allow boxes to be locked together and lifted, so that any manufacturer could use the design without payment. Only once every crane, lorry and railway wagon in the world could handle the same box did the system begin to show its real power.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences for ports were brutal. Container ships needed deep water, enormous cranes and acres of flat land for stacking, none of which the old city docks could offer. London and Liverpool, once among the busiest ports on earth, lost their trade to new terminals such as Felixstowe, a small harbour that had barely featured on the map. Manhattan's piers emptied as business moved across the bay to New Jersey. The workforce shrank as well. A gang that had needed a week to unload a ship was replaced by a handful of crane operators who could do it in a day, and tens of thousands of dockworkers lost their livelihoods despite strikes on both sides of the Atlantic.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The effect on manufacturing was slower but more profound. When transport was expensive, factories had to be near either their customers or their suppliers. As the cost of moving goods fell towards zero, that logic dissolved. A company could now design a product in one country, make its components in three others and assemble it in a fifth, choosing each location for its wages and skills. Economists who have tried to measure the impact suggest that the container did more to increase world trade than all the agreements on tariffs signed in the second half of the century.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The system is not without costs. Because inspecting every box would bring trade to a halt, only a small percentage are ever opened, which makes containers attractive to smugglers. Trade between regions is rarely balanced, so vast numbers of empty boxes must be shipped back to where they are needed. Each year some are washed overboard in storms and left to drift or sink. And the largest vessels, which now carry more than twenty thousand containers each, burn a heavy fuel that makes shipping a significant source of air pollution. The box solved the problem its inventor set out to solve. It also created a world that he could hardly have imagined.

passage.title: The conversation beneath the forest floor

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk through a forest and it is natural to see the trees as individuals, each competing with its neighbours for light and water. Over the past three decades, a body of research has suggested a very different picture, in which trees are linked below ground by fungi into networks that carry food and chemical signals from one plant to another. The idea has captured the public imagination. It has also provoked a sharp argument among scientists about how much of it is actually proven.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The partnership between trees and fungi is not in doubt, and it is ancient. The fine threads of certain fungi wrap around or enter the roots of a tree and spread out through the soil, reaching far beyond the roots themselves. The fungus is much better than the tree at collecting water and minerals such as phosphorus, and it passes some of these to its host. In return it receives sugars that the tree makes by photosynthesis, something the fungus cannot do. Around nine tenths of land plants are thought to depend on relationships of this kind.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The controversial step came in 1997, when the Canadian ecologist Suzanne Simard published the results of an experiment in the forests of British Columbia. She had exposed young birch trees to carbon dioxide containing a rare, traceable form of carbon, and later detected that carbon in neighbouring fir trees. Since a single fungus can be attached to many trees at once, the obvious explanation was that sugars were travelling through the fungal threads. The journal that published the paper put the story on its cover under a phrase that has been repeated ever since, the wood-wide web.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Later studies by Simard and others went further. Mapping the connections in one stand of fir, they found that the oldest and largest trees were linked to far more neighbours than the rest, and they came to be known as mother trees. It was proposed that these giants supported seedlings growing in deep shade, and even that they favoured their own offspring. Other researchers reported that a plant attacked by insects could send a warning through the network, prompting its neighbours to produce defensive chemicals before they were themselves attacked.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These claims have travelled a long way from the laboratory. They have featured in best-selling books and films, and they have been used to argue against the practice of felling the largest trees in managed forests. For many readers, the appeal lies in the suggestion that a forest is a cooperative community and not simply a battleground. Some foresters have changed their methods as a result, leaving old trees standing in the belief that they will nurture the next generation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In 2023, however, three ecologists who had themselves worked on fungal networks published a review of the evidence, and their conclusions were sobering. They accepted that carbon can move between trees, but pointed out that in most experiments the quantities were small, and that it was rarely possible to rule out other routes, such as movement through the soil. They found that the idea of large trees feeding seedlings was supported in fewer than a fifth of the field studies that had tested it, and that in some cases seedlings linked to a network actually grew worse. Most strikingly, by tracing how the original studies had been quoted in later papers, they showed that results described cautiously by their authors were often repeated by others as established fact.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means the networks are unimportant. Simard has replied that her critics underestimate the weight of the evidence, and that the benefits to seedlings may appear only in harsh conditions such as drought. The technical difficulty is real. Fungal threads are far thinner than a human hair, and a handful of forest soil may contain kilometres of them, so following a single molecule from one tree to another remains close to impossible. What the dispute illustrates is how readily an attractive scientific story can outrun the data, especially when it tells us what we would like to believe about nature.

passage.title: Does making choices wear us out?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 2011, a study of Israeli judges became one of the most widely quoted findings in psychology. Researchers analysed more than a thousand rulings made by parole boards and found a remarkable pattern. At the start of a session, prisoners were granted parole in about two thirds of cases. As the session went on, the rate fell steadily until it was close to zero, and then, after the judges had stopped for a meal, it jumped back to its starting level. The suggestion was that people who make one decision after another grow mentally tired, and that tired judges fall back on the safest option, which is to say no.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study seemed to confirm a theory that had been developing since the 1990s. The psychologist Roy Baumeister had proposed that self-control draws on a limited store of mental energy, rather as a muscle tires with use. In his best-known experiment, hungry students were seated in front of freshly baked chocolate biscuits and a bowl of radishes. Some were allowed the biscuits. Others were told to eat only the radishes. All were then given a puzzle which, unknown to them, had no solution. Those who had been made to resist the biscuits gave up on the puzzle in less than half the time. Resisting temptation, it appeared, had used up something they then lacked.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The idea had obvious attractions. It offered a scientific explanation for experiences everyone recognises, such as the shopper who compares prices carefully in the first aisle and throws anything into the trolley by the last. It was soon being applied to doctors, who were reported to prescribe unnecessary antibiotics more often late in a shift, and it was popularised by executives who said they wore the same clothes every day in order to save their mental energy for decisions that mattered.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Then the foundations began to crack. Psychology as a whole was discovering that many of its famous results could not be reproduced, and in 2016 a team coordinated across twenty-three laboratories repeated a standard test of Baumeister's theory with more than two thousand participants. They found an effect that was close to nothing. Baumeister objected that the task chosen was not the one he would have used, but a second large project, designed with the involvement of supporters of the theory, produced a result that was scarcely more encouraging.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The judges, too, came under scrutiny. Critics pointed out that the order in which cases were heard was not random. Prisoners without a lawyer, whose applications were weaker and more likely to fail, tended to be dealt with at the end of a session. Moreover, a judge who can see that the next case will be long and complicated may choose to stop for a break before it, so that sessions tend to end on quick refusals. A computer simulation showed that this kind of scheduling alone could generate the dramatic fall that the original authors had attributed to fatigue.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where does this leave the idea? Few researchers now defend the notion of willpower as a fuel that simply runs out. But it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing is going on. Studies of real behaviour over long periods, as opposed to brief laboratory tasks, do find that the quality of decisions changes through the day. One explanation that has gained ground is that the issue is motivation. After sustained effort, people do not lose the ability to concentrate. They become less willing to do so, and their attention drifts towards more rewarding activities. This would explain why experimental subjects who are paid, or who are told that willpower is unlimited, show no decline at all.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The episode carries a lesson that goes beyond one theory. The finding about the judges spread so quickly because it was vivid, easy to retell and consistent with what people already suspected about themselves. Those are precisely the qualities that ought to make us cautious. A result that is too neat, the story suggests, deserves more examination, not less.

passage.title: How the wolf came in from the cold

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The dog was the first animal that humans domesticated, long before sheep, cattle or horses, and it is the only one that was tamed by people who had not yet begun to farm. Beyond those two statements, almost everything about its origins has been disputed. When did it happen, where, and above all how did one of the most feared predators of the northern world become a creature that sleeps at the foot of the bed?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Genetic studies have settled one question. Every modern dog, from the smallest lapdog to the largest hound, descends from wolves, and not from jackals or some unknown wild dog as nineteenth-century naturalists supposed. The ancestor, however, was not the grey wolf that survives today but a population that has since died out. That makes dating the split difficult. Estimates based on DNA range from fifteen thousand to forty thousand years ago. The oldest remains that all experts accept as a dog come from a grave in Germany, about fourteen thousand years old, in which the animal was buried alongside a man and a woman.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The traditional explanation of what happened is that hunters took wolf cubs from the den, raised them, and bred from the most obedient. There are reasons to doubt it. Wolves reared by people remain unpredictable as adults, and a band of hunters would have had little reason to feed a large carnivore through a hard winter. Many researchers now prefer a second account, in which the wolves took the first step. Human camps produced bones and scraps. The animals bold enough to scavenge close to people, yet calm enough not to be driven away, ate better and left more offspring. On this view, the wolf domesticated itself, and only later did people take control of its breeding.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Support for the second account comes from a famous experiment that had nothing to do with wolves. In 1959, on a fur farm in Siberia, the Soviet geneticist Dmitri Belyaev began breeding silver foxes, choosing in each generation only the animals that showed least fear of a human hand. He selected for nothing else. Within ten generations, some foxes were wagging their tails and seeking out their keepers. More surprisingly, their bodies had changed as well. Patches of white appeared in the coat, ears drooped, and tails curled, features that are common in domestic animals of many species and almost unknown in their wild relatives. Tameness, it seemed, brought a whole set of other traits with it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Life beside people changed dogs in further ways. As farming spread, dogs came to eat what humans ate, and researchers have found that most dogs carry several extra copies of a gene involved in digesting starch, whereas wolves have only two. Their social intelligence altered too. In a much-repeated test, food is hidden under one of two cups and a person points to the correct one. Dogs, even young puppies, follow the gesture at once. Wolves raised by humans generally do not, and neither do chimpanzees, our own closest relatives.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A study published in 2019 added a curious detail. Dissecting the heads of dogs and wolves, anatomists discovered that dogs possess a small muscle that raises the inner eyebrow, and that in wolves this muscle is barely present. The movement makes the eyes look larger and gives the face an expression that people read as sad or appealing. Dogs in rescue shelters that made the movement more often were chosen by new owners more quickly. It is possible that, without knowing it, humans have for thousands of years favoured the animals whose faces they found hardest to resist.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be wrong, though, to imagine the partnership as one-sided. Early dogs gave warning of strangers and predators, helped to track and hold wounded game, and in the far north pulled loads across the snow. Some archaeologists have gone so far as to suggest that the alliance with dogs gave modern humans an advantage over the Neanderthals, who appear never to have formed one. That claim is far from proven. But it is a reminder that domestication changed both parties, and that the question of who tamed whom has no simple answer.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Seen from space, the earth is a blue planet, and yet water fit to drink is scarce. About ninety-seven per cent of the world's water is salt, and most of the remainder is locked in ice. As populations grow and rainfall becomes less reliable, a number of countries have turned to a solution that sailors and scientists dreamed of for centuries, which is to remove the salt from sea water. Today some three hundred million people depend, at least in part, on water produced in this way.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The oldest method simply copies nature. Sea water is heated until it evaporates, and the vapour, which leaves the salt behind, is cooled and collected as fresh water. Ships carried small stills of this kind from the eighteenth century onwards, and the first large plants, built around the Persian Gulf from the 1950s, worked on the same principle. The process is reliable and produces very pure water. Its weakness is that boiling water consumes enormous quantities of energy, which is why it took root in states that had oil and gas to spare.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The technique that now dominates the industry is quite different. In reverse osmosis, sea water is forced at very high pressure against a membrane, a thin sheet of plastic pierced by holes so small that water molecules can pass through while the larger particles of dissolved salt cannot. The principle was demonstrated in California in the late 1950s, but the early membranes let through only a trickle. Two developments turned it into a practical technology. Chemists learned to make membranes that were both thinner and tougher, and engineers devised machines that recover the pressure remaining in the waste water and use it to help push the next batch through. As a result, the electricity needed to produce a cubic metre of fresh water has fallen to about a quarter of what it was in the 1970s.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even so, desalination remains an expensive way of obtaining water. Its cost has come down to perhaps twice that of treating river water, and in most plants energy accounts for a third or more of the bill. Where that energy comes from burning fossil fuels, a technology adopted partly in response to a changing climate ends up contributing to the problem. Several countries have tried to break the link. A large plant near Perth in Australia buys its electricity from a wind farm built for the purpose, and new projects in the Middle East and North Africa are being paired with fields of solar panels.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The second environmental concern is what is left behind. For every litre of fresh water, a plant produces roughly a litre and a half of brine, which is about twice as salty as the sea and may contain chemicals used to keep the membranes clean. It is usually piped back into the ocean. Because brine is denser than sea water, it tends to sink and spread along the bottom, and in enclosed, shallow seas it can raise salt levels enough to harm the animals living on the sea bed. The damage can be limited by releasing the brine through a line of nozzles that mix it rapidly with the surrounding water, but this adds to the cost. Some researchers see the brine as a resource in its own right, a possible source of magnesium, lithium and other valuable minerals, although no one has yet shown that these can be extracted at a profit.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a risk at the other end of the pipe. The intakes that draw in sea water can suck in fish eggs, larvae and other small creatures in great numbers. Modern plants reduce the harm by taking water in slowly through fine screens, or by drawing it through wells drilled beneath the beach, so that the sand itself acts as a filter.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For all these reasons, most water engineers regard desalination as a last resort and not a first choice. Repairing leaking pipes, recycling waste water and persuading farmers to irrigate more efficiently will almost always deliver water more cheaply. Singapore, which has few natural supplies of its own, treats its waste water to such a standard that it can be returned to the taps, and turns to the sea for only a part of its needs. Yet for a coastal city in a dry region, the ocean has one overwhelming advantage. It is the only source of water that does not depend on the weather.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When people try to convey the scale of the changes brought by the internet, they often reach for a comparison with the invention of printing. The parallel is closer than it might seem. In the middle of the fifteenth century, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg brought together several existing technologies to create a machine that reproduced text mechanically. Within fifty years, the way that information moved around Europe had been transformed, with consequences that nobody at the time could have foreseen.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Printing itself was not new. In China, whole pages had been carved into wooden blocks and printed since at least the ninth century, and a craftsman named Bi Sheng had experimented with movable characters made of baked clay around 1040. The method suited Chinese poorly, however, since a printer needed thousands of different characters. An alphabet of two dozen letters made the idea far more practical. Gutenberg's real achievement was a hand-held mould in which identical metal letters could be cast quickly and in great numbers. He combined this with an oil-based ink that would stick to metal, and with a press adapted from those used for crushing grapes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The effect on the price and availability of books was dramatic. A scribe copying by hand might complete a few pages a day, and a single large volume could take a year. A printing shop could turn out several hundred copies of the same work in a few weeks. It has been estimated that more books were printed in the fifty years after Gutenberg than had been written out by all the scribes of Europe in the previous thousand. By 1500 there were presses in more than two hundred and fifty towns, and the price of a book had fallen by roughly two thirds.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The inventor himself did not profit. Gutenberg had borrowed heavily to finance his great Bible, and shortly before it was finished his principal backer, Johann Fust, took him to court to recover the debt. Gutenberg lost the case, along with much of his equipment, and Fust went on to run a successful printing business with one of Gutenberg's former assistants. It is a pattern that has been repeated many times since, in which the person who makes a technology possible is not the one who makes money from it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What people chose to print is revealing. The earliest printers relied on products with a guaranteed market, such as religious texts, Latin grammars for schoolboys and calendars. But the press quickly proved to be the ideal instrument for controversy. When Martin Luther challenged the authority of the Church in 1517, his supporters spread his arguments in short, cheap pamphlets, written not in Latin but in everyday German. Hundreds of thousands were in circulation within a few years. Earlier reformers had made similar criticisms and been silenced. Luther's ideas could not be contained, because they could be reproduced faster than they could be destroyed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Printing also changed knowledge in less obvious ways. Hand-copied books accumulated errors with every copy, so that no two were quite the same. Print made it possible for scholars in different cities to consult identical texts, diagrams and maps, and to refer one another to a particular page. Mistakes could be reported to the printer and corrected in the next edition. Some historians argue that this ability to fix, compare and gradually improve information was one of the conditions that made the scientific revolution possible.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It would be a mistake, though, to imagine that the new medium spread only truth. Printers needed to sell their stock, and sensational material sold well. Alongside Bibles and works of astronomy came forged documents, predictions of the end of the world, and lurid accounts of monstrous births and witches. Rulers and churches responded with lists of banned books and with systems of licences for printers, which were evaded almost as soon as they were introduced. The first information revolution, like the one we are living through, gave people access to more knowledge than ever before, and left them with the harder task of deciding what to believe.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Anyone who has walked from a sunlit car park into a wooded park on a summer afternoon knows that trees make a difference to temperature. As heatwaves become longer and more frequent, city governments around the world have seized on this familiar experience and turned it into policy. Mayors have pledged to plant millions of trees, and the proportion of a city shaded by leaves, known as its canopy cover, has become a standard measure of how well it is prepared for a hotter future. The enthusiasm is understandable. Whether the trees will deliver what is expected of them is a more complicated question.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Cities are warmer than the countryside around them, often by several degrees and most noticeably at night. The main cause is the materials from which they are built. Asphalt, brick and concrete absorb the sun's energy during the day and release it slowly after dark, while engines and air conditioners add heat of their own. Trees counter this in two ways. The first is shade, which prevents the ground and walls beneath from heating up. The second is less visible. A tree draws water from the soil and releases it as vapour through its leaves, and this evaporation uses up heat from the surrounding air, in the same way that sweat cools the skin.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Measurements confirm that the combined effect is substantial. Surveys using satellites have found that the surface of a tree-covered district can be ten degrees or more cooler than that of a neighbouring district of bare streets. It is important to be clear about what such figures mean, however. Satellites record the temperature of surfaces such as roofs and roads, not of the air at head height. When researchers carry thermometers through the streets, the difference in air temperature between leafy and treeless areas is usually much smaller, typically between one and three degrees.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even a modest reduction matters, because the relationship between heat and health is not gradual. Hospital admissions and deaths rise steeply once temperatures pass a certain point, and a degree or two can determine whether a night is cool enough for the body to recover. Studies in several countries have found that deaths during heatwaves are concentrated in districts with the least greenery. These are very often the poorest districts, where streets are narrow, gardens are rare and fewer households can afford air conditioning. For this reason, where trees are planted may be more important than how many.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Here the limits of planting campaigns become apparent. A newly planted tree offers almost no shade, and it may take twenty or thirty years to develop a full crown. In the meantime it has to survive conditions that are close to hostile. Its roots are confined to a small pit surrounded by compacted soil and buried pipes, rainwater runs off the paving into drains instead of soaking in, and salt, pollution and passing vehicles all do damage. In some cities, a third of street trees die within a few years of being planted. Counting the trees put in the ground, as most campaigns do, says very little about how much shade will exist a generation later.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is a further difficulty. The cooling that comes from evaporation depends on the tree having water. In a severe drought, which is exactly when heatwaves tend to occur, a tree closes the pores in its leaves to protect itself, and the effect largely stops. Shade continues, but the tree behaves more like a parasol than an air conditioner. The choice of species therefore matters a great deal. Trees that cope with dry conditions keep their leaves in a hot summer, but they often have small leaves and thin crowns, and so cast less shade than the broad-leaved species traditionally favoured for avenues.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this is an argument against planting. It is an argument for doing it carefully. The cities that have had most success tend to share certain habits. They protect the mature trees they already have, since a large tree lost to a building project cannot be replaced within a lifetime. They give new trees room, breaking up paving so that rain can reach the roots. They budget for watering and maintenance over many years, not just for the planting itself. And they combine trees with other measures, such as pale roofs and road surfaces that reflect sunlight, on the understanding that no single remedy will be enough.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Boredom has a poor reputation. Parents regard it as a problem to be solved, employers as a threat to productivity, and most of us as a state to be escaped as quickly as possible, usually by reaching for a phone. For a long time psychologists paid it little attention, perhaps because it seemed too trivial to study. In the past twenty years that has changed, and the picture emerging from their research is of an emotion that is both more harmful and more useful than was assumed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first task was to define it. Boredom is not the same as relaxation, which is pleasant, or as apathy, in which a person wants nothing. The bored person very much wants to be engaged in something satisfying and finds that nothing available will do. Researchers describe it as a failure of attention combined with a sense that the present activity lacks meaning. Time appears to pass slowly, and there is a restless urge to be somewhere else. It can arise when a task is too easy, but also, less obviously, when it is too hard, since in both cases the mind is unable to take hold.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How far people will go to avoid this state was shown by an experiment at the University of Virginia in 2014. Volunteers were left alone in an empty room for fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. The only object available was a device that delivered a mild electric shock, which they had already tried and had said they would pay to avoid. Two thirds of the men, and a quarter of the women, nevertheless pressed the button at least once. For many of them, an unpleasant sensation was evidently preferable to none at all.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The costs of boredom are well documented. People who say they are frequently bored are more likely to drink heavily, to gamble, to eat when they are not hungry and to take risks when driving. In schools, boredom predicts poor results at least as reliably as anxiety does. At work, it has been linked with mistakes in tasks that require long periods of monitoring, such as watching security screens or supervising automated machinery, where very little happens for most of the time and a lapse of attention can be disastrous.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why, then, would evolution have equipped us with such an emotion? The most persuasive answer is that boredom works as a signal, much as pain does. Pain tells us that the body is being damaged and prompts us to withdraw. Boredom tells us that our current activity is not worth the time and energy we are giving it, and pushes us to look for something better. An animal that was content to repeat the same unrewarding behaviour indefinitely would never have discovered new sources of food. On this view, boredom is not a defect but a mechanism that keeps us exploring.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers go further and claim that boredom encourages creativity. In one frequently cited study, people who had first spent fifteen minutes copying numbers out of a telephone directory went on to think of more uses for a plastic cup than people who had not. The suggestion is that an unoccupied mind begins to wander, and that a wandering mind makes unexpected connections. The evidence here is thinner than popular articles imply. Attempts to repeat such experiments have produced mixed results, and it may be that what helps is not boredom itself but the daydreaming that sometimes follows it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What does seem clear is that the outcome depends on how a person responds. Boredom creates a demand for change without specifying what the change should be. It can be satisfied by starting a project or by picking a quarrel. This is where the constant availability of entertainment on a screen becomes relevant. Scrolling removes the discomfort instantly, but it does so without supplying the sense of meaning whose absence caused the boredom in the first place. Several studies have found that people who turn to their phones whenever they feel bored report feeling more bored afterwards, not less. The emotion may be best treated neither as an enemy nor as a gift, but as a question that deserves a better answer than the nearest distraction.

passage.title: The machine that set people free

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The bicycle looks so obvious that it is tempting to assume it has always existed. In fact, it is younger than the steam locomotive, and it took most of the nineteenth century to reach the form we know. Its development is a useful corrective to the idea that inventions appear fully formed in the mind of a single genius. The bicycle was arrived at by trial and error, through a series of machines that were by turns absurd, dangerous and brilliant.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The story begins in Germany in 1817, when Baron Karl von Drais demonstrated what he called a running machine. It had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a handlebar for steering, but no pedals. The rider sat astride it and pushed against the ground with his feet. One theory holds that Drais was responding to a shortage of horses. A volcanic eruption in Indonesia two years earlier had darkened skies across the northern hemisphere, harvests had failed, and with oats too expensive to buy, many horses had starved or been slaughtered. Whether or not that was his motive, the machine was briefly fashionable among wealthy young men before being banned from the pavements of several cities.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Pedals arrived in Paris in the 1860s, fixed directly to the hub of the front wheel. This machine, with its iron tyres, was known in England as the boneshaker, and the name was earned. It also had a built-in limitation. Because one turn of the pedals produced exactly one turn of the wheel, the only way to travel faster was to make the wheel larger. The result was the high-wheeler of the 1870s, with a front wheel as tall as a man's chest and a tiny wheel behind. It was fast, and on the rough roads of the time its large wheel rolled easily over stones and ruts. It was also perilous. The rider sat almost directly above the axle, and a sudden stop could pitch him forward over the handlebars.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The solution, which appeared in the 1880s, was the so-called safety bicycle. Its two wheels were of equal and moderate size, and the rider sat between them, driving the rear wheel by means of a chain. Because the chain ran over a large toothed wheel at the pedals and a smaller one at the hub, a single turn of the pedals now carried the machine as far as a turn of the high-wheeler's giant wheel had done. Enthusiasts for the older machine mocked the newcomer as slow and undignified. They were silenced in 1888, when a Scottish vet living in Belfast, John Boyd Dunlop, fitted his young son's tricycle with tyres filled with air. The pneumatic tyre made the safety bicycle both more comfortable and faster than anything before it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What followed in the 1890s was a craze. Mass production brought prices down, and for the first time working people could afford a private means of transport that needed neither feeding nor stabling. The effects reached far beyond leisure. Clerks and factory hands could live further from their workplaces. Villagers could look for work, or for a husband or wife, beyond walking distance, and one geneticist has suggested that the bicycle did more than any other invention to widen the pool from which rural people chose their partners. Cyclists' organisations, meanwhile, campaigned loudly for smoother roads, and so prepared the way for the motor car that would later push them aside.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The bicycle's most celebrated social effect was on women. A machine that could not be ridden in a floor-length skirt and tight corset forced a change in what respectable women wore, and one that could be ridden alone allowed them to travel without a companion. Not everyone approved. Doctors warned of damage to health, and some writers of the day predicted moral collapse. The American campaigner Susan B. Anthony took a different view. Bicycling, she said in 1896, had done more to free women than anything else in the world.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In wealthy countries the bicycle went into decline once cars became affordable, and for decades it was regarded as a toy for children or a vehicle for those who could manage nothing better. Elsewhere it never lost its importance, and today well over a billion are in use around the world. In recent years it has returned to favour in the cities that once abandoned it, promoted as an answer to congestion, pollution and inactivity. The technology of the frame, the chain and the air-filled tyre has changed remarkably little since the 1890s. It would be hard to name another machine that was so nearly right so early.

passage.title: The current that warms a continent

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: London lies further north than Calgary, and Oslo further north than the southern tip of Greenland, yet the winters of north-western Europe are mild. Part of the explanation is simply that the prevailing winds blow in from the sea. But part of it lies in the ocean itself, in a vast system of currents that carries heat from the tropics towards the Arctic. Scientists know this system by a cumbersome technical name, and more informally as the Atlantic conveyor. There are signs that it is slowing down, and the question of what would happen if it weakened sharply has become one of the most closely watched in climate science.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The conveyor works because sea water is not all the same. Near the surface, a current that includes the Gulf Stream carries warm water northwards from the Caribbean. As it travels, it gives up heat to the air, and evaporation leaves it saltier. By the time it reaches the seas between Greenland, Iceland and Norway, the water is both cold and salty, which makes it unusually dense. It sinks, in places to a depth of several kilometres, and flows back towards the south along the ocean floor. Fresh surface water is drawn north to replace it, and so the circulation continues. The volume involved is enormous, about a hundred times the flow of the Amazon.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The weak point of this arrangement is the sinking. If the surface water in the far north becomes less salty, it becomes lighter, and it may no longer sink. That is exactly what a warming climate threatens to bring about. The ice sheet covering Greenland is melting at an increasing rate, and rainfall over the northern seas is growing, so that more and more fresh water is being added just where the conveyor is most sensitive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Evidence that this is no mere theory comes from the past. Layers of ice drilled from Greenland show that, as the last ice age was ending, temperatures there fell abruptly by as much as ten degrees within a few decades and stayed low for more than a thousand years. The most widely accepted explanation is that a huge lake of meltwater, held back by ice in North America, suddenly drained into the Atlantic and brought the conveyor almost to a halt. Mud from the sea bed supports the story. The size of the grains laid down on the ocean floor reflects the speed of the water passing over it, and at that period the grains become finer.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Measuring what is happening today is harder than it sounds. Since 2004, an array of instruments moored across the Atlantic between Florida and the coast of Africa has recorded the flow continuously. The readings show a decline, but they also show large swings from one year to the next, and two decades is too short a period to distinguish a lasting trend from natural variation. Researchers have therefore turned to indirect evidence. One clue is a patch of ocean south of Greenland that has cooled over the past century while almost everywhere else on the planet has warmed. If less warm water is arriving, this is precisely where a chill would be expected. On the basis of such evidence, several studies conclude that the conveyor is weaker now than at any time in the last thousand years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: How far the weakening will go is disputed. The computer models used by international climate bodies generally predict a gradual slowing over this century, not a collapse. However, a number of specialists argue that those models make the system appear more stable than it really is, and a statistical analysis published in 2023 caused a stir by suggesting that a tipping point could be reached before the middle of the century. Other experts replied that the data were too limited to support any date, and the matter remains unsettled.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The consequences of a collapse would be severe. Northern Europe would cool by several degrees even as the rest of the world went on warming, with harsher winters and far less rain for farming. Sea level along the east coast of North America would rise, because the current at present draws water away from that shore. The belt of tropical rain on which hundreds of millions of people in West Africa and South Asia depend would shift southwards. And such a change could not easily be undone. Once the sinking has stopped, the models suggest, cooling the planet again would not be enough to restart it for centuries.

passage.title: Finding islands in an empty ocean

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Pacific covers a third of the surface of the earth, and the islands scattered across its central and eastern parts are tiny and far apart. When European sailors first entered these waters in the sixteenth century, they were astonished to find almost every habitable island already occupied, by people who shared related languages and customs from New Zealand in the south-west to Hawaii in the north and Easter Island in the east. The Europeans themselves could cross the ocean only with compasses and charts, and many of them could not believe that others had done so without instruments. For a long time the favoured explanation was that the islands had been settled by accident, by fishermen blown off course in storms.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: That view is no longer taken seriously. Archaeology and genetics show that the settlers came from the west, moving out from the islands near New Guinea some three thousand years ago and reaching the most distant corners of the Pacific within the last thousand. They travelled against the prevailing winds, which is hardly the direction in which a drifting canoe would be carried. And they brought with them the plants and animals needed to start a new life, including taro, breadfruit, pigs and chickens. People who are blown out to sea by a storm do not usually have a farm on board.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A computer simulation carried out in the 1970s put the matter beyond doubt. Researchers released thousands of imaginary canoes from various islands and let them drift with the recorded winds and currents. Hardly any reached Hawaii, New Zealand or Easter Island. The settlement of those places must have been intentional. Sailing into the wind was in fact a sensible strategy for explorers. If no land was found before supplies ran low, the canoe could turn and be carried quickly home.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How, then, did the navigators find their way? Much of what we know comes from a handful of men in the islands of Micronesia who still practised the old methods in the twentieth century. The foundation was the stars. A navigator memorised the points on the horizon at which particular stars rise and set, and steered towards each in turn as it appeared, replacing it with the next when it climbed too high to be useful. A single night's course might require ten such stars, and a master navigator carried in his head the sequences for voyages to dozens of islands.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: By day, and under cloud, other signs were used. Ocean swells generated by distant weather systems keep a constant direction for days, and a skilled navigator could hold a course by the feel of the canoe as it rode over them, sometimes, it is said, lying down in the hull to sense the motion more exactly. Swells also bend around an island and bounce back from it, creating patterns of disturbed water that can be detected long before land is in sight.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Finding a small island at the end of a long passage was made easier by what has been called expanding the target. Certain seabirds fish at sea by day and return to land every night, so that birds seen flying purposefully at dusk point the way to shore from as far as fifty kilometres. Clouds gather and remain stationary over high islands. The underside of a cloud may take on a greenish tint above a shallow lagoon. By reading such signs, a navigator needed only to steer for a group of islands as a whole, a far larger objective than any single speck of land.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: By the middle of the twentieth century this knowledge had almost vanished from Polynesia itself. Its revival began in 1976, when a double-hulled canoe built in Hawaii to a traditional design sailed four thousand kilometres to Tahiti without instruments. No Hawaiian remembered the techniques, so the voyage was guided by Mau Piailug, a navigator from a tiny Micronesian island, who agreed to break with custom and teach outsiders because he feared the art would die with him. The canoe was met in Tahiti by a crowd of more than half the island's population. Its success ended the old argument, and it inspired a new generation across the Pacific to learn the skills of their ancestors.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Standard economic theory treats price as a continuous scale. A reduction from two dollars to one is supposed to have much the same effect on buyers as a reduction from one dollar to nothing. Shopkeepers have long suspected otherwise, and in the last two decades experiments have confirmed that zero is not just another price. Remove the final cent, and people behave as if a different set of rules applied.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The best-known demonstration was carried out by the behavioural economist Dan Ariely and his colleagues. At a stall in a university building they offered passers-by a choice between two chocolates, a luxury truffle at fifteen cents, far below its normal price, and an ordinary chocolate at one cent. Nearly three quarters chose the truffle, which was by any reasonable calculation the better bargain. The experimenters then lowered both prices by a single cent, so that the truffle cost fourteen cents and the ordinary chocolate was free. The difference in price between the two was exactly as before. Yet the preferences reversed, and more than two thirds of customers now took the free one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several explanations have been put forward. One is that every purchase, however small, carries a risk of regret, and that a free item appears to carry none. Another is that paying involves a moment of effort, in finding coins and weighing up value, which zero allows us to skip. A third is social. When money changes hands, we apply the standards of the market and ask whether we are getting a fair deal. When something is given, we shift to the standards that govern relations between friends, and calculation seems out of place.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The third explanation is supported by a study of what happens when the two sets of standards collide. A group of nurseries in Israel, troubled by parents who arrived late to collect their children, introduced a small fine. The number of late arrivals did not fall. It roughly doubled. Before the fine, parents who were late had felt guilty about inconveniencing the staff. The fine turned lateness into a service that could be bought, and at a very reasonable price. Most tellingly, when the nurseries abolished the fine after twelve weeks, the parents' behaviour did not return to what it had been. The sense of obligation, once replaced by a price, did not come back.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Businesses have learned to exploit the attraction of zero. An online retailer that offers free delivery on orders above a certain value finds that customers add items they do not need in order to qualify. When one such company introduced the offer across Europe, sales rose everywhere except in France, where, because of a local decision, delivery had been priced at the equivalent of a few cents instead of nothing. Sales there remained flat until the charge was removed. The few cents themselves were trivial. It was the difference between almost free and free that mattered.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The same logic underlies much of the digital economy. Services that cost billions to run are offered to users without charge, and the users, pleased with the bargain, seldom ask how the provider makes its money. The answer in most cases is that their attention and personal data are being sold to advertisers. Critics summarise the arrangement in a phrase that has become a commonplace, which is that if you are not paying for the product, you are the product. Whether people would make the same choice if the true exchange were stated plainly at the outset is a question the industry has shown little interest in testing.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that free is always a trap. Public health campaigns have used the effect to good purpose. In parts of Africa, charging even a small sum for mosquito nets treated with insecticide was found to reduce the number of families who obtained them by more than half, without making those who did pay any more likely to use them. Giving the nets away protected far more children. The lesson for policy is the same as the lesson for shoppers. A price of zero is a powerful tool, and it is worth asking, each time we meet it, whose purposes it is serving.

passage.title: Is the pen mightier than the keyboard?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In lecture halls around the world, the sound of pens on paper has largely been replaced by the tapping of keys. Students type faster than they write, their notes are easier to read and search, and nothing gets lost at the bottom of a bag. It seems an obvious improvement. Over the past decade, however, a series of studies has raised the possibility that something is lost when writing by hand disappears, both for adults taking notes and for children learning to read.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The study that started the debate was published in 2014 by two American psychologists, Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer. They asked students to watch recorded talks and take notes, some on laptops and some on paper, and then tested them. On questions of simple fact, the two groups did equally well. On questions that required an understanding of ideas, those who had written by hand did significantly better. When the researchers examined the notes, they found a likely reason. The typists had recorded far more words, and much of what they wrote was a word-for-word copy of what the speaker had said. The hand writers, unable to keep up, had been forced to select and to rephrase.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The interpretation was that slowness can be a virtue. To summarise an argument in your own words, you have to understand it first, and that effort of understanding fixes it in the memory. Taking down every word requires almost no thought at all. Strikingly, when a new group of laptop users was warned not to copy the speaker's words, they went on doing so anyway. The ease of typing seemed to invite it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The finding was widely reported, and some lecturers banned laptops as a result. Later research has complicated the picture. Several teams that repeated the experiment with larger numbers of students found a smaller advantage for handwriting, or none. They also pointed out that the original tests were given shortly after the talks. When students are allowed to go back over their notes before an examination, as happens in real courses, the fuller record produced by typing may be more useful than a brief summary. The fairest conclusion is perhaps that the way notes are taken matters more than the tool. A student who types a thoughtful summary will probably do as well as one who writes it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The evidence concerning young children is a good deal stronger. In experiments in the United States, children who had not yet learned to read were taught letters in one of three ways, by copying them with a pencil, by tracing over them, or by pressing the right key on a keyboard. Afterwards, those who had formed the letters freehand recognised them most accurately. Brain scans pointed in the same direction. When the children who had written the letters were later shown them, regions of the brain used by adults in reading became active. In the children who had typed, they did not.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why should the movement of the hand make such a difference? One suggestion is that each letter drawn by a child is slightly different from the last. Seeing many imperfect versions of a letter may teach the child what all of them have in common, and so what makes an A an A whatever the handwriting or typeface. A keyboard, by contrast, produces an identical letter every time, and pressing one key feels much like pressing another. A Norwegian team has reported that writing by hand produces more widespread patterns of electrical activity across the brain than typing does, of a kind thought to help in the formation of memories.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These results have had practical effects. Several countries and American states that had dropped the teaching of joined-up handwriting have reintroduced it. In Norway, where many schools issued tablets to pupils from the age of six, researchers have urged that children receive a minimum amount of instruction with pencil and paper. Not everyone is convinced the worry is justified. Critics observe that the long-term studies needed to show lasting harm have not been done, and that some children with difficulties in controlling a pen are liberated by a keyboard.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It is worth remembering that fears about the tools of writing are very old. Socrates is reported to have complained that writing itself would weaken the memory, since people would no longer need to carry knowledge in their heads. He was not entirely wrong, and yet few would wish writing uninvented. The sensible response to the keyboard is probably not to reject it but to be clear about what each tool is good for, and to make sure that children acquire both.

passage.title: The wolf, the elk and the willow

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the winter of 1995, fourteen grey wolves captured in Canada were released in Yellowstone National Park in the western United States. The species had been absent for almost seventy years, having been trapped, shot and poisoned out of existence by the park's own managers in the 1920s. Seventeen more animals followed the next year. The return of the wolf was the most closely studied experiment in the restoration of a predator ever attempted, and it gave rise to one of the best-loved stories in modern ecology. That story has since been questioned, and the argument over it shows how hard it is to establish cause and effect in the living world.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The story runs as follows. During the decades without wolves, the population of elk, a large deer, grew unchecked. In winter the elk gathered along the valley bottoms and ate the young willow, aspen and cottonwood trees until scarcely any survived to grow tall. When the wolves came back, they not only killed elk but frightened them. The elk began to avoid places where they could easily be trapped, such as river banks. Released from constant browsing, the trees recovered. Songbirds returned to nest in them. Beavers, which need willow for food and for building, came back and dammed the streams, creating ponds for fish and frogs. In the most popular version of the tale, the wolves even changed the course of the rivers, since banks held together by roots were less easily worn away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ecologists call a chain reaction of this kind a trophic cascade, and Yellowstone became its textbook example. A short film describing the changes has been watched more than forty million times. The appeal is obvious. The account suggests that nature, damaged by human interference, can repair itself if a single missing piece is restored.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Parts of the story are well supported. Elk numbers in the northern part of the park fell from around seventeen thousand in 1995 to fewer than five thousand fifteen years later, and in some places willows and aspens have indeed grown taller. The difficulties begin with the explanation. Wolves were not the only thing that changed. The number of grizzly bears and mountain lions, both of which kill elk calves, was rising over the same period. Hunters outside the park's boundary shot large numbers of elk until the rules were tightened in the mid-2000s. And a run of dry years reduced the growth of the grass on which the animals depend. Separating the influence of the wolves from all these other factors is far from simple.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The idea that fear alone altered the elk's behaviour has fared particularly badly. When researchers fitted elk with collars that recorded their position, they found that the animals did not in fact keep away from the areas where wolves were most active. They merely used them at times of day when the wolves were resting. Nor has the recovery of the trees been as general as early reports implied. One long-running study fenced off plots of willow to exclude elk completely. Even with no browsing at all, the willows grew well only where the researchers also built artificial dams to raise the level of water in the soil. Without beavers, the streams had cut deep channels, the ground had dried out, and removing the elk was not enough to reverse the change.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A further criticism concerns method. Some of the most quoted measurements were made by selecting the five tallest young aspens in each stand and recording their height. Since the tallest stems are, by definition, the ones that have escaped being eaten, sampling them was bound to exaggerate the recovery. When other teams measured stems chosen at random, the improvement they found was far more modest.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The scientists who first described the cascade continue to defend it, arguing that recovery is real but patchy, and slower than the popular version suggests. Their critics do not deny that predators matter. Their point is that an ecosystem which has been altered for seventy years may not simply spring back when one species is returned, because the damage has changed the landscape itself. Both sides tend to agree on a broader lesson. It is far easier to prevent the loss of a large predator than to undo the consequences afterwards.

passage.title: The network that shrank the world

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the morning of 24 May 1844, Samuel Morse sat in the chamber of the Supreme Court in Washington and tapped out a short message on a metal key. Sixty kilometres away in Baltimore, his assistant received it almost at once and sent it back. For the whole of human history until that moment, with trivial exceptions such as signal fires and flags, information had been able to travel no faster than a horse or a ship. Within a generation, it would circle the globe in minutes. The electric telegraph has some claim to be the most disruptive communications technology ever introduced, more so than the telephone or the internet that followed it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Morse was not a scientist. He was a portrait painter who had become interested in electricity during a sea voyage, and the idea that a current could carry a signal along a wire had occurred to several people before him. In Britain, William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone had a working system a few years earlier, in which needles on a dial pointed to letters. What Morse and his collaborator Alfred Vail contributed was simplicity. Their apparatus needed only a single wire, and their code represented each letter by a combination of short and long pulses. Vail is said to have visited a printer's workshop and counted the pieces of type in each compartment, in order to give the shortest codes to the letters used most often.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first customers were the railways, which needed to know where their trains were, and the wires were strung along the tracks. Newspapers and merchants soon followed. Before the telegraph, the price of wheat or cotton in one city could differ greatly from the price in another, and a trader who received news a day ahead of his rivals could make a fortune. Afterwards, prices in distant markets moved together. Newspapers that had filled their columns with reports weeks old began to compete to print events of the previous day, and agencies were founded to gather news and sell it by wire to many papers at once.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The greatest challenge was the ocean. In 1858, after several failed attempts, a cable was laid across the bed of the Atlantic between Ireland and Newfoundland, and Queen Victoria exchanged greetings with the American president. The celebrations were premature. The signal was so weak that the queen's message of ninety-eight words took sixteen hours to transmit, and when an engineer tried to improve matters by raising the voltage, he burned through the insulation. The cable went dead after three weeks. A lasting connection was not made until 1866, using a heavier cable and the largest ship then afloat to carry it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Contemporaries greeted the new network with the kind of hope that would later be attached to the internet. Instant communication between nations, it was said, would make misunderstanding impossible and war a thing of the past. The reality was less tidy. Governments quickly grasped that control of the cables meant power. Britain, whose companies owned most of the world's undersea lines, used them to direct its empire and, in wartime, to read or cut the messages of its enemies. The network also created new kinds of crime. Fraudsters bribed operators to delay or alter messages about prices, and codes had to be devised to keep commercial information secret.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The telegraph changed language, too. Because messages were charged by the word, senders learned to strip out everything unnecessary, producing a clipped style that left its mark on journalism. It has been suggested that the plain, compact prose of some twentieth-century novelists, several of whom began as reporters, owes something to the discipline of the wire.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There was also a social dimension that is easily forgotten. The operators who worked the lines formed a community of their own. They recognised one another by the rhythm of their tapping, exchanged gossip and jokes during quiet hours, played chess over the wire, and occasionally fell in love with colleagues they had never met. A good number of them were women, for whom telegraphy was among the first technical occupations open. The network they served was replaced in its turn, by the telephone and then by newer systems. But the pattern it established, of exaggerated hopes, commercial upheaval, new crimes and new forms of friendship, has been repeated with every communications technology since.

passage.title: Do we all see the same rainbow?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: English speakers divide the visible spectrum into about eleven basic colours, and it is easy to assume that these divisions are facts about the world. They are not. Russian has two separate words where English has only blue, one for the light shade and one for the dark, and a Russian speaker would no more call them varieties of one colour than an English speaker would describe pink as a kind of red. Some languages make far fewer distinctions. The question of why languages differ in this way, and whether the differences affect what their speakers actually see, has occupied linguists and psychologists for more than a century.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the prevailing view was that the spectrum is a continuous band which each language cuts up as it pleases. This was taken as strong support for the theory that language shapes thought. If the lines between colours are drawn by vocabulary and not by nature, then people who speak different languages might be said to inhabit different visual worlds.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That view was challenged in 1969 by two American researchers, Brent Berlin and Paul Kay. They showed speakers of twenty languages a chart of several hundred coloured chips and asked them to pick out the best example of each basic colour word in their language. The boundaries between colours varied a good deal from one language to another. The best examples, however, were remarkably similar. Whatever the language, the purest red or the purest green fell on nearly the same chips.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Berlin and Kay made a second and more surprising claim. Languages, they said, acquire colour words in a fixed order. A language with only two terms divides colours into roughly dark and light. If it has a third, the third is always red. Next come green and yellow, in either order, and then blue. Only after that do terms such as brown, purple, pink and orange appear. A language with a word for purple but none for red is, on this account, never found. The original study was based on a small number of speakers, most of them living in California, and it was heavily criticised. But a much larger survey of over a hundred languages spoken in non-industrial societies broadly confirmed the pattern, though with more exceptions than the authors had first allowed.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why should red come first? One explanation appeals to biology. The human eye is particularly sensitive to red, which is the colour of blood, ripe fruit and the faces of people who are angry or embarrassed. A more recent proposal looks to usefulness. Analysing thousands of photographs, researchers found that objects people want to talk about, such as food, animals and tools, tend to be warm in colour, while backgrounds such as sky, water and foliage tend to be cool. Languages may therefore develop precise words for reds and yellows before they bother to separate green from blue. Supporting this, it is in industrial societies, where manufactured objects come in every imaginable colour, that vocabularies are largest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this settles whether words influence perception, and here the Russian blues have proved useful. In an experiment at an American university, volunteers were shown three blue squares and asked which of the lower two matched the one above. When the two squares fell on opposite sides of the boundary between the Russian words, Russian speakers answered faster than when both belonged to the same category. English speakers showed no such difference. The advantage disappeared when the Russians were asked to repeat a string of numbers silently while doing the task, which suggests that they were, without realising it, using language to help them judge.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The effect is real, but it should not be exaggerated. It amounts to a fraction of a second, and it does not mean that English speakers are unable to see the difference between light and dark blue. The Himba people of Namibia, whose language groups certain greens with blue, were said in a television documentary to be unable to pick out a blue square among green ones. The claim spread widely online, but the test shown in the film was a dramatisation, and published studies of the Himba report only that they are somewhat slower at such tasks, not blind to the difference.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The picture that has emerged satisfies neither extreme. Colour vocabulary is not arbitrary, since it is limited by the eye and shaped by what communities need to discuss. Nor is it irrelevant to thought. The words we learn as children seem to nudge our attention, making some differences a little easier to notice than others. We all see the same rainbow, but we do not all draw its stripes in the same places.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Whenever the price of some asset rises to absurd heights, from internet shares to digital currencies, journalists reach for the same comparison. In the Dutch Republic in the winter of 1636 to 1637, the story goes, an entire nation lost its senses over tulips. Bulbs changed hands for the price of a house, chimney sweeps and maids gambled their savings, and when the market collapsed in February 1637, thousands were ruined and the economy was plunged into depression. It is a wonderful tale. According to historians who have gone back to the archives, a good deal of it is untrue.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The tulip reached the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire in the late sixteenth century, and it arrived in a country well prepared to prize it. The Dutch were then the richest people in Europe, their merchants had money to spend on luxuries, and the flower was unlike anything in northern gardens. The most sought-after varieties were not of a single colour but streaked with flames of crimson or purple on a white ground. We now know that these patterns were caused by a virus carried by aphids, which also weakened the plant. A prized bulb therefore produced few offspring, and since nobody understood the cause, nobody could produce the effect to order. Rarity was built in.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For several decades the trade was confined to wealthy collectors, who paid high prices in much the same spirit as they paid for paintings. The change came in the mid-1630s. Because tulips flower only briefly in spring and the bulbs lie in the ground for most of the year, a custom grew up of buying and selling during the winter by means of written promises to pay when the bulbs were lifted. These contracts could themselves be sold on. Dealers met in the back rooms of taverns, and a single bulb might pass through several hands, on paper, without anyone seeing it. In the last weeks of 1636, prices for some varieties rose twentyfold.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The peak came in the first days of February 1637. At an auction in the town of Alkmaar, held for the benefit of the orphaned children of an innkeeper, a collection of bulbs fetched ninety thousand guilders, at a time when a skilled craftsman earned perhaps three hundred a year. Days later, at a routine sale in Haarlem, no buyers appeared. The news spread, confidence vanished, and within a week the trade had stopped.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What happened next is where the legend parts company with the evidence. The historian Anne Goldgar spent years examining the legal and financial records of the period, looking for the victims. She found very few. She could not identify a single person who had been made bankrupt by tulips. The buyers and sellers turned out to be a fairly small group of merchants and prosperous craftsmen, many of them related or connected through their churches, and not the chimney sweeps of the legend. And because the contracts had required no money in advance, most were simply never honoured. After months of quarrelling, the authorities in Haarlem allowed buyers to cancel on payment of a small percentage of the agreed price. The wider Dutch economy showed no sign of injury and went on to its most prosperous decades.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Where, then, did the famous version come from? Much of it can be traced to pamphlets printed in 1637 by religious moralists, who seized on the affair as a warning against greed and against the confusion of social ranks. Their colourful inventions, including the sailor who ate a priceless bulb in mistake for an onion, were intended as satire. Two centuries later, the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay repeated them as fact in a best-selling book about popular delusions, and it is from Mackay that most modern accounts descend.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This is not to say that nothing happened. Prices did rise beyond all reason and did collapse, and the episode shook people who had believed that their neighbours' word could be relied upon. Goldgar suggests that the real damage was to trust, not to wealth. Economists continue to argue over whether the prices were ever irrational. Some point out that rare bulbs kept their value for years afterwards, and that it was only the common varieties, traded by newcomers in the final weeks, that became worthless.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The lasting interest of tulip mania may lie less in what it tells us about markets than in what it tells us about stories. A moral tale invented for one purpose proved so satisfying that it survived for four hundred years, and it is still quoted, with complete confidence, by people warning others not to believe everything they hear.
