passage.title: The end of an easy century

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In September 1928, the bacteriologist Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to his laboratory in London and noticed that a mould had contaminated one of his culture dishes. Around the mould, the bacteria he had been growing had died. The substance responsible, which he named penicillin, was eventually turned into a medicine by a team at Oxford during the Second World War, and it changed human life. Infections that had killed routinely, after a scratch from a rose thorn or the birth of a child, became trivial. Operations such as hip replacements and organ transplants, which expose patients to dangerous bacteria, became possible. It is estimated that antibiotics have added about twenty years to average life expectancy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Fleming himself foresaw the danger. Accepting the Nobel Prize in 1945, he warned that bacteria exposed to too small a dose could be educated to resist the drug. He was describing evolution in action. In any large population of bacteria, a few individuals may by chance carry a mutation that lets them survive an antibiotic. When the drug kills their competitors, the survivors multiply to fill the space. Bacteria reproduce so quickly, some of them every twenty minutes, that a resistant strain can become dominant within days. They have a further trick. Unrelated species of bacteria can pass genes directly to one another, so that resistance which arises in a harmless microbe in the gut may be handed to a deadly one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Every use of an antibiotic therefore gives resistance an opportunity, and for decades the drugs were used with extraordinary freedom. Doctors prescribed them for colds and sore throats, most of which are caused by viruses on which they have no effect at all. In many countries they could, and still can, be bought over the counter without a prescription. The greatest quantities, however, have not been given to people. Farmers discovered in the 1950s that animals fed small regular doses grew faster, and by some estimates three quarters of the antibiotics sold in the world are still used on livestock, much of it on animals that are not ill.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For a long time none of this seemed to matter, because whenever a drug began to fail there was another to replace it. Between the 1940s and the 1960s, more than twenty new classes of antibiotic were introduced. Then the supply dried up. Hardly any truly new classes have reached patients since the 1980s. The reasons are partly scientific, since the compounds that were easy to find have been found, and partly commercial. Developing a drug costs well over a billion dollars. A company can recover that sum from a medicine for blood pressure, which a patient may take daily for thirty years. An antibiotic is taken for a week, and a new one would deliberately be kept in reserve and used as little as possible in order to delay resistance. Most large pharmaceutical firms have closed their antibiotic research departments.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The consequences are already visible. A study published in 2022 estimated that infections resistant to treatment were directly responsible for about one and a quarter million deaths worldwide in a single year, more than malaria. Forms of tuberculosis have emerged that respond to none of the standard drugs. Hospitals in several countries have reported patients infected with bacteria that no available antibiotic can kill. If the trend continues, routine surgery could again become a gamble.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What can be done? The first step is to waste less. Countries that have restricted the use of antibiotics in farming have seen levels of resistance in animals fall, in the Netherlands by more than half, without the predicted damage to their farmers' incomes. Rapid tests that tell a doctor within minutes whether an infection is caused by bacteria or by a virus would prevent many unnecessary prescriptions. Simple hygiene matters as well, since every infection that is prevented is one that does not need treating.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: New drugs will still be needed, and governments have begun to experiment with ways of paying for them. Under a scheme being tried in Britain, the health service pays a company a fixed annual fee for access to a new antibiotic, regardless of how much is used, in the way one might subscribe to a streaming service. The aim is to reward the invention without rewarding sales. Researchers are also returning to older ideas. One is the use of viruses that attack bacteria, a treatment developed in the Soviet Union before antibiotics made it seem unnecessary. Another is to search for new compounds in unexplored places, from deep-sea mud to the nests of ants.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Whatever succeeds, the underlying lesson is uncomfortable. Antibiotics are not like other medicines, which work as well for the thousandth patient as for the first. Their power is a shared resource that is used up a little with every dose, and the choices made by one patient, one farmer or one country affect everyone else.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the savannahs of southern Africa, mounds of hard red earth rise from the ground to twice the height of a person. They are the work of termites, insects a few millimetres long and almost blind, and relative to the size of their builders they are the tallest structures made by any animal. A single mound may house a million individuals. What has drawn engineers and architects to study them, however, is not their size but the way they manage air.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The species that build the largest mounds do not eat wood directly. Deep within the nest they cultivate a fungus on beds of chewed plant material, and the fungus breaks the material down into food. This arrangement, together with the breathing of the insects themselves, uses as much oxygen as a large mammal such as a goat and produces carbon dioxide in proportion. Without constant ventilation, the colony would suffocate. The termites and their fungus are also sensitive to temperature and to drying out, in a climate where the air may be close to freezing at dawn and above forty degrees by mid-afternoon.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For many years the accepted explanation of how the mound copes was put forward by a Swiss scientist, Martin Luscher, in the 1960s. He suggested that the mound works like a chimney. Air warmed by the colony rises through a central shaft, cools as it passes through thin-walled channels near the surface, where it also exchanges gases with the outside, and then sinks back to the nest. The interior was said to be held at an almost constant thirty-one degrees.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This account inspired one of the most frequently cited examples of design borrowed from nature. The Eastgate Centre, an office and shopping complex that opened in Harare, Zimbabwe, in 1996, has no conventional air conditioning. Its architect, Mick Pearce, gave it heavy masonry walls that absorb heat by day, and a system of fans that flush the building with cool night air, which is then drawn up through the floors and out by way of tall chimneys on the roof. The building is reported to use about a tenth of the energy of a comparable block cooled by machinery, and its tenants pay lower rents as a result.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It later emerged that the termites do not behave quite as Luscher had supposed. From the 1990s onwards, the American biologist Scott Turner and his colleagues filled mounds with tracer gas, inserted probes, and in some cases poured in plaster and washed away the soil to reveal the network of tunnels. They found no steady circulation driven by the heat of the nest. Nor was the temperature inside constant. It followed the temperature of the surrounding soil through the seasons, which the mound's own bulk kept stable from hour to hour. The exchange of gases, Turner concluded, depends chiefly on wind. Gusts striking the mound set up small, fluctuating differences in pressure across its porous outer wall, pushing air in and out through a mesh of fine tunnels, rather as breath moves in and out of a lung.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: More recent measurements suggest a third mechanism in some species. During the day the thin outer ridges of the mound warm faster than its core, and at night they cool faster, so that the air inside turns over once every twenty-four hours. Probably all three processes operate to different degrees in different places. What they have in common is that the structure exploits small, freely available differences in temperature and pressure, and that none of them requires a moving part.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The discovery that the Eastgate Centre was based on a mistaken idea has not made the building any less successful, and it has encouraged a second wave of experiments. Engineers are now testing walls of porous material, perforated like the surface of a mound, which would allow a building to exchange air gently with the outside without draughts and without fans.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The most intriguing question is how the mound comes to be built at all. No termite has a plan of it, and none directs the others. Each individual follows a few simple rules. A worker tends to deposit its pellet of soil where other pellets have recently been placed, and it is stimulated to build or to dig by local levels of moisture and carbon dioxide. Where the air is stale, the insects open passages. Where it is too dry, they seal them. Out of millions of such small acts, a structure emerges that is continually adjusted to the needs of the colony. For designers interested in buildings that could repair and adapt themselves, the method may prove more instructive than the mound.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1652, a servant from the eastern Mediterranean named Pasqua Rosee opened a stall selling coffee in an alley in the City of London. The drink was a novelty, black, bitter and served scalding hot, and many who tried it compared it to soot. Within a decade there were more than eighty coffee houses in the capital, and by the end of the century several hundred. They changed not only what Londoners drank but how they did business, exchanged news and argued about ideas.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To appreciate the change, it helps to remember what people had been drinking before. Water in towns was often unsafe, and the usual alternative, even at breakfast, was weak beer. Much of the population passed the working day in a mild alcoholic haze. Coffee offered something quite new, a drink that was safe because the water had been boiled, and that sharpened the mind instead of dulling it. Its admirers were quick to draw the contrast between the noisy, quarrelsome tavern and the sober, industrious coffee house.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The coffee house was also unusual in the company it admitted. For the price of a penny, any man who was reasonably dressed could enter, take a seat at one of the long shared tables, and join the conversation, whatever his rank. A printed set of rules displayed in some establishments declared that no one need give up his place to a finer gentleman. Visitors from abroad were struck by the spectacle of lords and tradesmen sitting side by side. The equality had limits. The poor could not spare the penny or the time, and although women frequently owned and served in coffee houses, they were not generally welcome as customers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What customers bought with their penny was, above all, information. Coffee houses took in the newspapers and pamphlets of the day and left them on the tables, and some employed a boy to read aloud for the benefit of those who could not read. A man could learn in an hour what was being said in Parliament, on the docks and in foreign capitals. It was this, more than the coffee, that earned them the nickname of penny universities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Different houses attracted different trades, and several grew into institutions that still exist. Shipowners and sea captains gathered at the house kept by Edward Lloyd, who collected reliable news of arrivals and losses for their benefit. Merchants who were willing to share the risk of a voyage signed their names beneath the details of the ship, and from this practice developed the insurance market that bears Lloyd's name. Dealers in shares, expelled from the Royal Exchange for rowdiness, met at Jonathan's, the forerunner of the London Stock Exchange. Men of science adjourned from meetings of the Royal Society to continue their discussions over coffee. It was in the course of one such argument, the story goes, that the astronomer Edmond Halley was prompted to ask Isaac Newton a question about planetary orbits, the answer to which grew into the most famous book in the history of physics.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone was pleased. Tavern keepers resented the competition, and a satirical petition published in 1674 in the name of the women of London complained that coffee kept their husbands from home and made them good for nothing. The most serious opponent was King Charles II. His father had been overthrown and executed, and he regarded places where men gathered freely to read the news and criticise the government as nurseries of rebellion. In December 1675 he issued a proclamation ordering every coffee house to close. The outcry was immediate, and the proclamation was withdrawn after eleven days, before it had even come into force.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The great age of the London coffee house lasted little more than a century. Some of the most successful turned themselves into private clubs, open only to members, and so lost the very openness that had made them distinctive. And from the early eighteenth century the country's tastes were shifting towards tea, which the East India Company imported in growing quantities and which, unlike coffee, could easily be prepared at home.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Historians have been tempted to see in the coffee house the birthplace of modern public opinion, a space outside the control of court and church in which private individuals reasoned together about public affairs. The claim needs some qualification, given how many were excluded. It is nevertheless striking how often the coffee house is recalled in discussions of the internet, as an earlier experiment in bringing strangers together to share information, with a similar mixture of commerce, enlightenment, rumour and alarm.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A playground built today in most wealthy countries looks very different from one built fifty years ago. The tall metal slide, the roundabout that could be spun until children flew off, and the climbing frame set in concrete have gone. In their place are low platforms, enclosed tube slides and a carpet of rubber. The change was made with the best of intentions, to protect children from injury. A growing number of researchers now argue that it has gone too far, and that in removing risk from play we have removed something children need.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The modern safety movement can be dated with some precision. In the United States in the late 1970s, a series of lawsuits brought by the parents of injured children resulted in very large payments, and official guidelines followed, specifying the maximum height of equipment and the surfaces to be laid beneath it. Local councils, schools and manufacturers, anxious to avoid being sued, complied. Similar standards spread to Britain, Australia and much of Europe. One consequence was that playgrounds everywhere began to look alike, since few designers dared to depart from the catalogue.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whether children became safer is less clear than might be expected. Rubber surfaces do reduce head injuries from short falls. But in several countries the overall number of children treated in hospital after playground accidents has not fallen since the standards were introduced, and for broken arms it has in some places risen. One explanation offered is that a soft surface makes both children and the adults watching them less careful. Another is boredom. Children who find the equipment too tame use it in ways that were never intended, climbing on the outside of the tube slide or onto the roof of the playhouse.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most influential critic has been the Norwegian psychologist Ellen Sandseter. After observing and interviewing children in nurseries, she identified six kinds of risky play that children everywhere seek out. They are play at great heights, play at high speed, play with dangerous tools, play near dangerous elements such as fire or water, rough-and-tumble play such as wrestling, and play where there is a chance of getting lost. In each case, she observed, children approach the danger gradually. A child climbs a little higher each day, feeling a mixture of fear and excitement, and stops at the point where the fear becomes too great.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Sandseter's argument is that this is precisely how fears are overcome. Almost all young children are afraid of heights, and most are not by the time they are adults. What happens in between is repeated, self-directed exposure. In support of this, a long-running study in New Zealand found that children who had been injured in a fall before the age of nine were less likely, not more, to be afraid of heights at eighteen. A child who is never allowed to climb, on this view, is not protected from fear but left alone with it. There is evidence, too, that rough-and-tumble play teaches children to control aggression, since a game of wrestling continues only as long as both players hold back.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These ideas have found practical expression in the adventure playground, a type that first appeared in Denmark in the 1940s. A landscape architect had noticed that children ignored the playgrounds he designed and played on building sites instead, and he proposed giving them a plot of land, a pile of scrap timber and some tools. Trained staff are present, but their job is to intervene as little as possible. At one such playground in Wales, children build dens, light fires and roll down a hill inside old tyres. Researchers who have compared accident records report that injury rates at adventure playgrounds are no higher than at conventional ones, and some insurers charge them lower premiums.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of the researchers in this field argue that children should be exposed to real hazards. The distinction they draw is between a risk, which a child can see and judge, and a hazard, which is hidden. A high branch is a risk. A rotten branch is a hazard. The task of adults is to remove the second while leaving the first. A number of official bodies have accepted the point. Guidance issued in Britain now asks those who provide playgrounds to weigh the benefits of an activity against its dangers, instead of simply eliminating danger.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Change on the ground has been slower. Parents who accept the argument in principle may still be reluctant to let their own child climb a tree, and a school that permits it risks being blamed if something goes wrong. The deeper difficulty is that an injury in the playground is visible and immediate, while the cost of a childhood without challenge, whether in anxiety, in physical inactivity or in a lack of confidence, is spread over many years and cannot be traced to any one decision.

passage.title: The ground that is no longer frozen

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Across the far north of Russia, Canada and Alaska, and on the high plateau of Tibet, lies ground that has not thawed for thousands of years. It is known as permafrost, and it underlies roughly a quarter of the land in the northern hemisphere. In places it is more than a kilometre deep. For as long as people have lived on it, it has been treated as solid rock. Roads, pipelines, airports and entire cities have been built on the assumption that it would stay hard. That assumption is beginning to fail.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Permafrost is defined simply as ground that remains at or below freezing for at least two years in a row. It is not all ice. It is a mixture of soil, gravel and sand held together by ice, and above it lies a shallower layer that thaws each summer and freezes again each winter. Plants grow in this upper layer, and when they die their remains decay only partly before the cold preserves them. Over tens of thousands of years, an enormous store of dead plant material has accumulated in the frozen ground beneath. Scientists estimate that it contains about twice as much carbon as the whole of the atmosphere.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The Arctic is now warming three to four times faster than the planet as a whole, and the frozen ground is responding. As the summer thaw reaches deeper, material that has been locked away since the last ice age is exposed to microbes, which begin to digest it. Where oxygen is present, they release carbon dioxide. In waterlogged ground, where it is absent, they release methane, a gas that traps far more heat over the short term. The gases warm the climate, the warming thaws more ground, and so the process feeds itself. This is what researchers mean when they describe permafrost as a feedback.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: How large the effect will be is one of the major uncertainties in forecasts of the climate. Early alarm centred on the idea of a sudden, catastrophic release, sometimes called a methane bomb. Most specialists now think this unlikely. Their concern is a steady leak that continues for centuries and cannot be switched off. Current estimates suggest that thawing permafrost could release as much greenhouse gas over this century as a large industrial country. A complication is that warmer conditions also allow more plants to grow in the north, and growing plants absorb carbon. For a time, in some regions, this may offset part of the loss.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Recent fieldwork has revealed that thaw does not always proceed gradually from the top down. Where the ground contains large bodies of ice, melting causes the surface to collapse, forming pits and slumps that can deepen by several metres in a few years. Water gathers in the hollows and speeds the thaw beneath. Such abrupt collapse affects only a small part of the permafrost region, but because it exposes deep, ancient material so quickly, it may account for a large share of the gases released. The models used for global projections have until recently left it out.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For the four million people who live on permafrost, the consequences are immediate. Buildings in Siberian cities stand on concrete piles driven into the frozen ground, and as it softens they tilt and crack. A survey has suggested that most buildings in some Russian Arctic towns are already damaged. In 2020, a fuel tank at a power station near the city of Norilsk collapsed when its supports sank, spilling twenty thousand tonnes of diesel into nearby rivers. In Alaska, villages on eroding coasts are being moved inland at great expense. Engineers can keep the ground cold beneath a structure by installing devices that draw heat out of the soil in winter, but these are costly and protect only what stands directly above them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The thaw is also uncovering the past. Frozen carcasses of mammoths and other ice-age animals emerge from river banks, and a trade in mammoth tusks has grown up in Siberia. More disturbingly, microbes can survive in a frozen state for a very long time. In 2016, an outbreak of anthrax on a peninsula in northern Russia, which killed a child and thousands of reindeer, was traced to the body of a reindeer that had died of the disease decades earlier and had been exposed by an unusually hot summer.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Unlike the burning of coal and oil, the release of carbon from permafrost cannot be regulated by any government. The only way to limit it is to limit the warming that causes it. That is why many scientists argue that the frozen north, remote as it is, should be given far more weight when international targets for emissions are set.

passage.title: A computer from the ancient world

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the spring of 1900, a party of Greek sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera discovered the wreck of a Roman cargo ship. It had gone down in about 60 BC, loaded with bronze and marble statues, glassware and coins. Among the treasures brought to the surface over the following months was a shapeless lump of corroded bronze and wood, about the size of a large book. It attracted little notice until, as it dried, it split apart to reveal the remains of toothed wheels. Nothing remotely like it had ever been found from the ancient world, and for half a century most scholars did not know what to make of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious study was made in the 1950s by a British historian of science, Derek de Solla Price. Using X-ray photographs, he counted the teeth on the surviving wheels and concluded that the device was a kind of mechanical calculator for following the movements of the sun and moon. His claim was greeted with scepticism. It was widely believed that the Greeks, for all their brilliance in mathematics, had lacked the practical skill to build precise machinery, and gearing of this complexity is not otherwise known in Europe until the cathedral clocks of the fourteenth century. A few writers even suggested that the object must have fallen onto the wreck from a much later ship.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The doubts were settled in the first decade of the present century, when an international team examined the eighty-two surviving fragments with two new techniques. One was a powerful X-ray scanner, weighing eight tonnes, which had to be transported to the museum in Athens because the fragments were too fragile to be moved. It produced three-dimensional images of the interior. The other was a method of photographing surfaces under light from many different angles, which made faint scratches readable. Together they revealed thousands of tiny Greek letters, hidden for two thousand years, which amounted to an instruction manual engraved on the machine itself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: From this evidence the function of the mechanism has been reconstructed in detail. It was housed in a wooden case with a handle on the side. Turning the handle moved the date forward on a dial at the front, and at least thirty interlocking bronze wheels drove pointers showing the position of the sun and moon in the sky and the phase of the moon. On the back, two spiral dials followed longer cycles. One was a calendar of nineteen years, the period after which the phases of the moon fall on the same days of the year. The other predicted eclipses, and indicated the time of day at which each would occur.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Two features have particularly impressed modern engineers. The Greeks knew that the moon appears to move across the sky at a varying speed, faster at some points in the month than at others. The maker reproduced this by mounting one gear slightly off-centre on another and linking them with a pin sliding in a slot, so that the output speeded up and slowed down in the correct rhythm. And a small dial among the others had nothing to do with astronomy at all. It showed the four-year cycle of the athletic games, including those at Olympia, which were the basis of the Greek system for numbering years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whether the device also displayed the movements of the five planets known in antiquity is less certain, since the relevant wheels are lost. The inscriptions, however, name the planets and give the periods of their cycles, and in 2021 a team in London published a design showing how the necessary gears could have fitted in the space available. Their model works, but it remains a proposal and not a proven reconstruction.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Who made the mechanism is unknown. The style of the lettering suggests a date in the second century BC. The names of the months on the calendar are those used in Corinth and its colonies, which has led some researchers to link it with the tradition of Archimedes, who lived in the Corinthian colony of Syracuse and is reported by Roman writers to have built a model of the heavens. Others favour the island of Rhodes, a centre of astronomy from which the ship may have sailed.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The deepest puzzle is why so sophisticated an object stands alone. A machine of this quality cannot have been the first of its kind, and ancient authors do mention similar devices. Yet none has survived. The likeliest explanation is mundane. Bronze was valuable and was routinely melted down for reuse, so that an instrument which was no longer wanted simply became raw material. The Antikythera mechanism was preserved only because it was lost. It is a sobering thought that our whole picture of ancient technology would be different if one ship had reached its harbour.

passage.title: When many heads are better than one

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1906, the English scientist Francis Galton visited a country fair where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and prepared. About eight hundred people paid for a ticket and wrote down a figure. Some were butchers and farmers. Many had no special knowledge at all. Galton, who had a low opinion of the judgment of ordinary people, borrowed the tickets afterwards and worked out the average of the guesses. It came to 1,197 pounds. The ox weighed 1,198. The crowd, taken as a whole, had been more accurate than almost any individual in it, including the experts.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation is statistical. Each person's guess can be thought of as containing two parts, some real information and some error. If the errors are of different kinds, with some people guessing too high and others too low, they tend to cancel one another when the guesses are combined, while the information accumulates. The same principle has been confirmed in many settings since. Groups of students asked to estimate the number of sweets in a jar, the temperature of a room or the distance between two cities reliably produce an average that is closer to the truth than the great majority of the individual answers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The idea was brought to a wide audience in 2004 by the American writer James Surowiecki, and it has been put to practical use. Some companies run internal markets in which employees bet small sums on questions such as whether a product will be finished on time, and the prices in these markets have often proved better forecasts than the official plans. Forecasters of elections and of the weather routinely average the predictions of many models and find the result more accurate than that of the best single one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Surowiecki was careful to point out that crowds are wise only under certain conditions. The first is diversity. The members must draw on different information or see the problem from different points of view, since a crowd of people who all think alike will share the same errors. The second is independence. Each person must reach a judgment without knowing what the others have decided. The third is some means of gathering the individual judgments into a collective one, whether an average, a vote or a market price.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It is the second condition that most often fails. A group of Swiss researchers asked volunteers to estimate figures such as the length of a border or the number of crimes committed in a year. When the volunteers were then told what others had guessed and allowed to revise their answers, the range of estimates narrowed sharply as people moved towards one another. The average, however, did not become more accurate. Worse, the participants grew more confident in their answers precisely as those answers became less independent. Knowing what others think, it appears, reduces the diversity on which the whole effect depends, while persuading everyone that they must be right.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This helps to explain why groups that meet to discuss a question frequently do worse than the same individuals polled separately. The first person to speak, or the most senior, sets a direction that others are reluctant to contradict. Financial bubbles can be understood in the same way, as occasions on which investors stop judging the value of an asset for themselves and start judging what other investors will do. For this reason, some organisations now ask members of a committee to write down their views before a meeting begins, and to hear from the most junior person first.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There is a further limit. The averaging of guesses works for questions that have a definite answer, a number or a yes or no. It is much less clear that a crowd can design a bridge, compose a piece of music or decide what a society ought to value. And a crowd that is collectively ignorant, with errors that all lean the same way, will be confidently wrong. Had the visitors to the fair been asked to estimate the weight of the moon, their average would have been worthless.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One curious finding suggests that the principle can be applied by a single mind. In an experiment, people were asked a factual question and then, some weeks later, asked the same question again without warning. The average of each person's two answers was closer to the truth than either answer alone. The benefit was smaller than that of asking a second person, but it was real. The effect has been called the crowd within, and the practical advice that follows from it is very old. Before committing yourself to a judgment, sleep on it and guess again.

paragraphs.text: Deep inside a mountain on the Arctic island of Spitsbergen, eight hundred miles from the North Pole, a tunnel runs for more than a hundred metres through solid rock to three chambers kept at eighteen degrees below zero. On the shelves are sealed foil packets containing more than a million samples of seed, sent by nearly every country on earth. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, which opened in 2008, has been called a doomsday vault, and it is often imagined as a means of replanting the earth after some global catastrophe. Its real purpose is more modest, and more practical.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To understand it, one has to begin with the way farming has changed. For most of the ten thousand years since agriculture began, farmers saved their own seed from each harvest, and over generations every valley came to have its own varieties of wheat, rice or beans, adapted to the local soil and weather. In the twentieth century, plant breeders produced new varieties that gave far heavier crops, and farmers across the world adopted them. Yields rose enormously. The cost was uniformity. It has been estimated that three quarters of the genetic variety of crops was lost from farmers' fields during the century, and today a large share of the world's food comes from a handful of closely related strains.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The danger of this was shown in the United States in 1970, when a fungus destroyed around a seventh of the country's maize in a single season. Almost all the maize being grown shared one inherited feature that happened to make it vulnerable. The remedy was found in older varieties that lacked the weakness. Breeders constantly need such material, to resist a new disease, to tolerate drought or salt, or to ripen in a shorter season. Old varieties and the wild relatives of crops are their library, and once a variety is no longer planted anywhere, the only place it survives is a collection.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are about seventeen hundred such collections, or gene banks, around the world. Seeds are dried, sealed and frozen, and in that state most will stay alive for decades. They cannot be stored indefinitely, however. Every so often a sample must be taken out, tested, and if necessary sown, so that fresh seed can be harvested to replace the old. This work is expensive, and many national gene banks are short of money. Freezers break down. Buildings flood. The gene banks of Afghanistan and Iraq were destroyed in war, and that of the Philippines was damaged first by a typhoon and then by fire.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Svalbard was conceived as a backup for all the others. A gene bank sends duplicates of its seeds, which remain its own property and can be withdrawn only by the bank that deposited them. The Norwegian government paid for the construction and charges nothing for storage. The location was chosen with care. The site is remote yet can be reached by scheduled flights, it lies well above the highest predicted level of the sea, and the surrounding rock is permanently frozen, so that if the cooling machinery failed, the chambers would warm only slowly and would remain below zero for many years.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The first withdrawal came sooner than anyone had expected. An international centre based near Aleppo in Syria held one of the world's most important collections of wheat, barley and lentils from the region where farming began. As the civil war closed in, the staff managed to send copies of most of the collection to Svalbard before the centre had to be abandoned. In 2015 the organisation asked for its seeds back. They were planted at new sites in Lebanon and Morocco, multiplied, and used to rebuild the working collection, and fresh duplicates have since been returned to the vault.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The vault has had problems of its own. In the unusually warm winter of 2016, rain fell instead of snow, and meltwater ran into the entrance tunnel and froze there. No seeds were harmed, since the water came nowhere near the chambers, but the incident was an embarrassment for a building designed to last for centuries, and the tunnel has since been rebuilt in waterproof concrete.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Some specialists warn against placing too much faith in frozen collections. A seed in a freezer does not go on adapting, whereas a crop growing in a field continues to evolve with its pests and its climate. Many important food plants, among them bananas, potatoes and cassava, are not normally grown from seed at all, and have to be kept alive as plants or as tissue in a laboratory. And a packet of seed is of little use without the knowledge of the farmers who grew it. For these reasons, most experts regard gene banks as one half of a strategy. The other half is to support the farmers who still grow traditional varieties, so that diversity is kept alive in the field as well as in the cold.

passage.title: The roads that outlasted an empire

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the height of its power, in the second century AD, the Roman Empire was held together by something like eighty thousand kilometres of paved highway, with several times that length of lesser roads branching from it. The network ran from the north of Britain to the edge of the Sahara and from the Atlantic to the river Euphrates. No state would build anything comparable until the nineteenth century. Many modern European roads still follow Roman lines, and in a few places the original paving remains in use.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first great road, the Via Appia, was begun in 312 BC to link Rome with the south of Italy, and its purpose was plainly military. A legion marching on a paved road could cover thirty kilometres a day in any weather, with its baggage, and arrive in a condition to fight. As Rome's territory expanded, roads followed the armies, and in many provinces they were built by the soldiers themselves, partly, it was said, to keep them out of mischief in peacetime.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Roman roads are famous for running straight, and the reputation is deserved, though it needs some qualification. The surveyors laid out a route as a series of straight sections between points that could be seen from one another, such as hilltops, and changed direction where one section met the next. They worked with a simple sighting instrument, a cross of wood from which weighted strings were hung, and with signal fires for long distances. Where the land was level, a road might not bend for fifty kilometres. In mountains, engineers were perfectly willing to follow the shape of the ground.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The method of construction varied with the materials to hand, but the principle was constant. A trench was dug down to firm ground and filled in layers. Large stones went in at the bottom, then smaller stones or rubble, often bound with lime, then gravel, and on the most important roads a surface of fitted stone blocks. The finished road was higher in the middle than at the edges, so that rain ran off into ditches at either side. It was this attention to drainage, above all, that made the roads last. Water lying in a road freezes, expands and breaks it apart, and Roman engineers understood that a dry road is a durable one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Along the main highways the state maintained a service that had no equal until modern times. Stations where fresh horses were kept stood every fifteen kilometres or so, with larger rest houses offering beds and food at intervals of a day's journey. The system existed for official business, and a courier carrying government dispatches could change horses repeatedly and cover eighty kilometres in a day, far more in an emergency. Private travellers needed a permit to use it, although such permits were frequently obtained by influence or forged. Stone pillars at every mile recorded the distance to the nearest town and the name of the emperor who had built or repaired the road.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Whatever their original purpose, the roads quickly acquired others. Merchants used them, though for heavy goods transport by water remained far cheaper, and it has been calculated that carrying grain a hundred kilometres overland could double its price. Ideas travelled more easily than cargo. Latin spread along the roads, as did Roman law, fashions in building, and in time the Christian religion, whose early missionaries moved from city to city on the imperial highways. The same roads carried disease. Epidemics that began in one province reached others with a speed that had not been possible before.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Recent research suggests that the influence of the network did not end with the empire. A team of economists compared a map of Roman roads with satellite photographs of Europe at night, in which the intensity of light is a rough guide to economic activity. Areas that had been well served by roads two thousand years ago were, on average, more prosperous today. The researchers argue that towns grew up at junctions and river crossings, that later roads and railways were laid along the same routes, and that an early advantage was thus handed down. Significantly, they found no such pattern in North Africa and the Middle East. There, wheeled vehicles were largely abandoned in favour of camels after the empire's fall, the old roads were no longer maintained, and the link between ancient roads and modern prosperity disappears.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It is tempting to see the roads simply as a triumph of engineering. They were also an expression of power, built with the labour of conquered peoples and designed to let an army reach any rebellious province quickly. An ancient historian put a bitter remark about Roman rule into the mouth of a British chieftain, to the effect that the conquerors created a desert and called it peace. The roads remind us that the same structure can be at once an instrument of control and a gift to later generations.

passage.title: The sea is no longer silent

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The French explorer Jacques Cousteau called his famous film about the ocean The Silent World. The title could hardly have been less accurate. Water carries sound far better than air, and the sea has always been full of it, from the crack of breaking ice and the rumble of earthquakes to the calls of whales and the snapping of shrimps. What has changed in the last hundred years is the addition of a new layer of sound made by people. In parts of the ocean, the background level of noise has doubled in every decade since the 1960s, and biologists are increasingly concerned about what this means for the animals that live there.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To see why noise matters so much under water, one has to appreciate how limited the other senses are. Light fades quickly with depth, and even in clear water an animal can rarely see more than a few tens of metres. Smell disperses slowly. Sound, by contrast, travels almost five times faster in water than in air and can cross entire ocean basins. Many marine animals therefore rely on hearing as land animals rely on sight. Fish grunt and drum to attract mates. Dolphins find their prey by producing clicks and listening for the echoes. The low calls of blue and fin whales could once be heard by others of their species across hundreds, perhaps thousands, of kilometres.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The largest source of human noise is shipping. The world's fleet of merchant vessels has grown more than fourfold since 1950, and the main sound a ship makes comes not from its engine but from its propeller. As the blades turn, they create bubbles that collapse with a continuous low roar. This noise is concentrated at exactly the frequencies used by the great whales. It has been estimated that the distance over which a whale's call can be heard has shrunk by nine tenths in some regions. Animals that once kept in contact across an ocean may now be unable to find one another across a bay.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Other sources are more intense but less constant. Ships searching for oil and gas beneath the sea bed tow arrays of air guns that release blasts of compressed air every ten seconds or so, for weeks on end. These are among the loudest sounds people produce. The driving of steel piles into the sea bed for wind farms and harbours makes a similar noise, and naval sonar has been linked on several occasions with groups of whales swimming onto beaches.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Evidence of harm has been accumulating. Whales have been observed to stop feeding, change their routes and raise the volume of their calls when ships are near. An accidental experiment was provided by the days after 11 September 2001, when shipping off the east coast of North America was sharply reduced. Scientists who happened to be collecting the droppings of right whales in a Canadian bay found that the level of stress hormones in the samples had fallen markedly, and it rose again when traffic returned. Effects are not confined to large animals. Young fish searching for a reef on which to settle are guided by its sound, and in noisy water fewer of them arrive. Even shellfish and squid have been found to be injured by loud sound.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is, however, one encouraging feature of noise that sets it apart from most forms of pollution. Plastic and chemical waste remain in the sea for decades or centuries. Noise stops the moment its source is switched off, and it leaves nothing behind. This means that action has an immediate result.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Much could be done at modest cost. Because the noise of a propeller rises steeply with speed, a ship that slows by a fifth can cut the sound it makes by more than half, and it burns less fuel as well. A trial in the waters off Vancouver, in which ships were asked to slow down while passing through an area used by killer whales, showed that most captains were willing to comply. Propellers can be redesigned so that fewer bubbles form. Around construction sites, a hose laid on the sea bed can release a rising curtain of air bubbles, which absorbs much of the sound of pile-driving before it spreads.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The obstacle is the lack of rules. Shipping is regulated by an international body which has issued guidelines on quieter ship design, but they are voluntary, and few owners have followed them. Scientists who study the problem argue that noise should be treated like any other pollutant, with limits that can be enforced. They point out that when the world's shipping slowed during the pandemic of 2020, the oceans grew measurably quieter within weeks. It was a glimpse of what the sea used to sound like, and of how quickly it could be restored.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every human society that has ever been studied has music. People sing to their babies, at their weddings and at their funerals, and they do so in cultures that have had no contact with one another. Flutes carved from the bones of birds and from mammoth ivory, found in caves in southern Germany, are more than forty thousand years old. Yet music has no obvious use. It does not feed or shelter anyone. Charles Darwin called the human capacity for it one of the most mysterious with which our species is endowed, and scientists have been arguing about its origin ever since.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One camp holds that music is an accident. The best-known statement of this position came from the psychologist Steven Pinker, who compared music to cheesecake. We did not evolve to enjoy cheesecake. We evolved to seek out fat and sugar, which were scarce and valuable to our ancestors, and cheesecake happens to deliver both in a concentrated form. In the same way, on this view, music exploits mental abilities that evolved for other purposes, above all for language, and gives us pleasure without doing us any good.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Others think music is too ancient, too universal and too costly in time and effort to be a mere by-product. Darwin himself proposed that it began as a means of attracting a mate, as birdsong does. A more widely supported suggestion today is that it binds groups together. When people sing or move in time with one another, experiments show, they afterwards feel closer, cooperate more readily and tolerate more pain, a sign that the brain's natural painkillers have been released. For our ancestors, living in bands that depended on cooperation, such an effect could have meant the difference between survival and failure. A further proposal looks to the nursery. Mothers in all cultures sing to infants in a recognisable style, slow and high and repetitive, and the practice may have begun as a way of calming a child that had to be put down while the mother worked.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The study of the brain has not settled the argument, but it has shown how deeply music reaches. Listening to a piece we love activates the same reward system that responds to food and other pleasures. Using scanners, researchers in Montreal found that the chemical dopamine is released at the emotional high point of a piece, and also, in a different part of the brain, during the seconds leading up to it. Much of the pleasure of music, it seems, lies in anticipation. Composers build expectations and then delay, confirm or defeat them, and a listener's brain is constantly making predictions about what will come next.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Music also has an unusual relationship with memory. Most people can recall the words of songs they learned as children far more accurately than anything they were taught in a classroom, and a few notes of a tune can bring back a scene from decades earlier with startling vividness. This persists even when other memories fail. Patients with advanced dementia who no longer recognise their own families will often sing along to the songs of their youth, and become calmer and more responsive while they do. The regions of the brain that store familiar music appear to be among the last to be damaged by the disease.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These findings have encouraged the use of music in medicine. People who have lost the power of speech after a stroke can sometimes still sing, because song and speech are handled partly by different areas of the brain, and a therapy based on singing phrases has helped some of them to talk again. Patients with Parkinson's disease, who have difficulty beginning a movement, often walk more steadily to a strong beat.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Rather less well founded is the belief that music makes people more intelligent. A small experiment in 1993 reported that students performed slightly better on one kind of puzzle after listening to Mozart for ten minutes. The effect lasted about a quarter of an hour. It was nonetheless reported around the world, and one American state began giving a recording of classical music to every newborn child. Later work showed that the improvement came from being in a good mood, and that a lively story read aloud did just as well.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The claim that learning an instrument sharpens the mind is harder to dismiss, but it faces the difficulty that children who take lessons differ from those who do not in many ways, including the income and education of their parents. In the few studies that assigned children to music lessons at random, the gains in other subjects were small. The best reason to learn an instrument may simply be the one that needs no experiment to support it, which is that making music is one of the oldest pleasures we have.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of history, the question of whether planets circle other stars was a matter for philosophers. The stars are so distant, and planets so faint beside them, that looking for one was compared to trying to spot a moth fluttering beside a searchlight from thousands of kilometres away. Then, in 1995, two Swiss astronomers announced that they had detected a planet in orbit around a star similar to the sun, about fifty light years away. In the three decades since, more than five thousand planets beyond our solar system have been confirmed, and astronomers now believe that planets outnumber stars.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Swiss discovery was made without anyone seeing the planet at all. A planet does not simply circle a stationary star. The two bodies pull on each other, and the star moves in a small circle of its own. Seen from earth, it sways slightly towards us and away again, and this motion produces tiny, regular shifts in the colour of its light. Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz measured such shifts in a star called 51 Pegasi and inferred that something with about half the mass of Jupiter was tugging it to and fro every four days.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The result was startling, and at first it was doubted. In our own system the giant planets lie far from the sun and take years to complete an orbit. A giant that circled its star in four days, closer than Mercury is to the sun and heated to a thousand degrees, was something no theory had predicted. Astronomers had assumed that other planetary systems would resemble ours. It soon became clear that ours might be the unusual one. Such hot Jupiters were simply the easiest planets to detect, since a massive planet in a tight orbit makes its star sway most.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second method has since proved even more productive. If a planet's orbit happens to carry it across the face of its star as seen from earth, it blocks a small fraction of the light, and the star dims by a tiny amount at regular intervals. The method demands extraordinary precision, since a planet the size of earth crossing a star like the sun reduces its brightness by less than one part in ten thousand. A space telescope named Kepler, launched in 2009, was designed to stare without interruption at a single patch of sky containing about a hundred and fifty thousand stars. Over nine years it found more than two and a half thousand planets.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Kepler's results allowed astronomers to estimate, for the first time, how common different kinds of planet are. The most numerous type turned out to be one that our solar system lacks altogether, with a size between that of earth and Neptune. Whether such planets are rocky worlds with thick atmospheres, or balls of water and gas, is still unclear. Kepler also showed that small planets are abundant. A substantial fraction of stars are thought to have a planet of roughly earth's size orbiting at a distance where water could exist as a liquid on the surface, neither frozen nor boiled away, a region sometimes called the habitable zone.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The term should be treated with caution. It describes only the distance from the star, and says nothing about whether a planet actually has water, air or anything else that life might require. Venus lies near the inner edge of our own sun's habitable zone and has a surface hot enough to melt lead. Many of the candidate planets circle small, dim red stars, which are prone to violent flares that could strip away an atmosphere.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The next step is to study the atmospheres of these worlds directly. When a planet passes in front of its star, a little of the starlight filters through the thin layer of gas around it, and each gas absorbs particular colours, leaving a pattern like a bar code in the light that reaches the telescope. Using this technique, the James Webb Space Telescope has identified carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane in the atmospheres of several planets. The ultimate aim is to find a combination of gases that is hard to explain without living things. On earth, oxygen and methane exist together only because plants and microbes constantly replace them. Left alone, they would react with each other and vanish.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Even such a discovery would be difficult to interpret, since chemistry without biology can sometimes produce the same gases, and several announcements of possible signs of life have already been withdrawn after further analysis. Most researchers expect that the first claim to be widely accepted will rest not on a single observation but on many kinds of evidence gathered over years. What has changed is that the question is no longer one for philosophers. For the first time, we have the instruments to look.

passage.title: From precious metal to drinks can

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At a banquet in Paris in the 1850s, the emperor Napoleon III is said to have honoured his most distinguished guests by serving them with plates and cutlery of aluminium, while the rest of the company had to make do with gold. When the Washington Monument was completed in 1884, it was capped with a small pyramid of the same metal, then as costly as silver. Within a few years of that date, the price had collapsed, and today aluminium is the material of drinks cans and kitchen foil. No other substance has travelled so far, so fast, from luxury to the commonplace.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The paradox is that aluminium was never rare. It is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust, making up about eight per cent of it by weight, and it is present in common clay. The difficulty is that it is never found as pure metal. It binds so tightly to oxygen that the methods used for centuries to extract iron or copper, heating the ore with charcoal, have no effect on it. A Danish scientist first separated a few impure grains in 1825, using chemical reactions, and for the next sixty years the metal could be produced only in small quantities and at great expense.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The breakthrough came in 1886, and it came twice. In Ohio, a twenty-two-year-old chemistry graduate, Charles Martin Hall, working in a shed behind his family's house, found that if aluminium oxide was dissolved in a molten mineral called cryolite and a strong electric current passed through the liquid, pure metal collected at the bottom. A few weeks later, in France, Paul Heroult, who was the same age and knew nothing of Hall, filed a patent for the identical process. By a further coincidence, the two men, born in the same year, also died in the same year. The method they discovered is still the one used in every aluminium smelter in the world.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The process needed two other developments to become practical. One was a cheap way of obtaining aluminium oxide from the reddish rock known as bauxite, which an Austrian chemist, Karl Bayer, devised soon afterwards. The other was electricity in very large quantities, which only became available with the building of power stations in the 1880s and 1890s. One of the first great smelters was constructed beside Niagara Falls to take advantage of the power generated there. The price of aluminium fell by more than ninety-five per cent in a decade.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The properties of the metal soon found uses. It weighs about a third as much as steel. Exposed to air, it does not rust away but forms a thin, hard film that protects the metal beneath. Mixed with small amounts of copper and other elements, it becomes strong enough to carry heavy loads. The engine of the aircraft in which the Wright brothers made the first powered flight in 1903 had a casing of aluminium, chosen to save weight, and the growth of aviation and of the aluminium industry went hand in hand from then on. During the Second World War, the public were urged to hand in their saucepans to be melted down for aircraft.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The cost of all this is energy. Producing a tonne of aluminium from ore consumes about as much electricity as an average household uses in several years, and smelting accounts for a noticeable share of the world's consumption. For this reason, smelters have traditionally been built where power is cheap and not where the ore is mined or the metal is used. Iceland, which has abundant hydroelectric and geothermal power but no bauxite at all, imports the raw material by ship from the other side of the world and exports the finished metal. The mining of bauxite, mostly in the tropics, leaves behind large quantities of caustic red mud, which has to be stored behind dams.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Against this must be set a remarkable advantage. Aluminium can be melted and reused indefinitely without loss of quality, and recycling it requires only about five per cent of the energy needed to make it from ore. It has been estimated that three quarters of all the aluminium ever produced is still in use. A drinks can that is collected may be back on a shop shelf, as a new can, within sixty days. Rates of collection vary greatly, however. Where a small deposit is charged on each can and refunded when it is returned, as in Germany and parts of Scandinavia, well over nine in ten are recovered. Where there is no such scheme, more than half may end up buried in the ground.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Demand for the metal is expected to rise considerably in the coming decades, partly because lighter vehicles use less fuel and partly because solar panels and power cables require it. Whether that demand can be met without a large increase in emissions will depend on two things, which are the source of the electricity that smelters use, and how much of the aluminium already in circulation can be persuaded to come back.

passage.title: The return of the wooden tower

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the centre of a small Norwegian town stands a building eighteen storeys and eighty-five metres high. It contains flats, a hotel, offices and a swimming pool, and its columns, beams and floors are made almost entirely of wood. When it was completed in 2019 it was the tallest timber building in the world, a title it has since lost to a tower in the American city of Milwaukee. Taller ones are planned. After a century in which steel and concrete were the only materials considered for large buildings, architects are returning to the oldest of all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What has made this possible is not ordinary timber but a family of products known as engineered wood. The most important is made by laying boards side by side in a sheet, gluing a second layer on top at right angles to the first, and repeating the process until a solid panel is formed, which may be as much as thirty centimetres thick and the size of a lorry. Because the grain runs in two directions, the panel is strong both along its length and across it, and it does not swell or shrink as a single plank would. The technique was developed in Austria and Germany in the 1990s, originally as a way of using up low-grade timber for which sawmills had little market.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first objection people raise is fire. It is a natural one, and the answer is surprising. A thin stick burns readily, as anyone who has lit a campfire knows, but a thick log does not. When the surface of a large piece of timber burns, it forms a layer of char which insulates the wood beneath and slows the fire's progress to well under a millimetre a minute. A heavy timber beam can therefore go on carrying its load in a fire for longer than an unprotected steel beam, which does not burn but softens and bends when it grows hot. Engineers design timber structures with extra thickness that can be sacrificed, and full-scale tests, in which furnished rooms have been set alight and left to burn, have persuaded the authorities in a number of countries to raise the height permitted for wooden buildings.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The chief attraction for those who commission such buildings is environmental. The manufacture of cement and steel is responsible for a substantial share of the world's emissions of carbon dioxide. A tree, by contrast, absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows, and roughly half the dry weight of wood is carbon, which stays locked in a building for as long as the building stands. Studies comparing similar buildings suggest that a timber structure is responsible for between a quarter and a half less carbon than a concrete one.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There are practical advantages too. The panels are cut to size in a factory by machines following a digital model, with openings for windows and pipes already made, and are delivered to the site in the order in which they will be needed. They are then lifted into place and screwed together. A floor can be completed in days. Because a timber building weighs perhaps a fifth as much as a concrete one, its foundations can be smaller, and far fewer lorries are needed to deliver the materials. A site in a crowded city is quieter, cleaner and occupied for a shorter time.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The claims made for the material are not accepted by everyone. The environmental benefit depends on where the wood comes from. If a forest is cut down and not replanted, or if old forest that has stored carbon for centuries is replaced by young plantations, the calculation changes entirely. Researchers have also pointed out that only part of each tree ends up in a building, and that if the rest is burned or left to rot, its carbon returns to the air. And the benefit is lost if, at the end of the building's life, the timber is simply sent to be burned. Supporters reply that the wood should come only from forests certified as being replanted, and that buildings can be designed to be taken apart so that the panels are used again.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Other difficulties are more ordinary. Wood must be kept dry during construction, since panels that are soaked by rain may later grow mould. Sound passes more easily through a light floor than a heavy one, so that extra layers are needed between flats. Insurers, with little experience of the material, sometimes charge more to cover it. And in most countries timber still costs somewhat more than concrete, though the speed of building recovers part of the difference.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: No one expects wood to replace steel and concrete altogether. The very tallest towers and the longest bridges are likely to remain beyond it, and most of the timber buildings now going up are in fact hybrids, with a concrete core containing the lifts and stairs. The more realistic prospect is of a change in the middle range, the blocks of six to twelve storeys that make up the bulk of a modern city. If even a modest proportion of those were built of timber, the effect on the construction industry's emissions would be considerable.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the Pacific island of New Caledonia lives a crow that has overturned a good deal of what scientists believed about animal intelligence. It is an unremarkable bird to look at, black and about the size of a pigeon. But it does something that, apart from humans, is known in only a handful of species. It not only uses tools. It manufactures them, to a pattern, and it appears to improve on the design.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The crows feed on grubs that live deep in holes in rotting wood, out of reach of a beak. To get at them, a bird breaks off a twig, strips away the side branches and leaves, and pokes it into the hole. The grub bites the end of the twig in defence and is drawn out. More remarkably, the crows make hooks. A bird selects a forked twig, snaps it just below the fork, and then trims and shapes the stump with its beak until it forms a neat barb. A second kind of tool is cut from the long, tough leaves of a tree whose edges are lined with backward-pointing spines. The crow tears out a strip that is wide at one end, where it is held, and tapers in steps to a narrow point.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What makes these leaf tools especially interesting is that their design differs from one part of the island to another. In some regions crows make only wide strips, in others narrow ones, and in others the stepped kind. The differences do not correspond to any difference in the trees or the prey. Researchers believe that young crows learn the local method from their elders. Juveniles stay with their parents for a year or more, watch them at work, and practise with the tools their parents have discarded. If so, this is a tradition passed from one generation to the next, something very close to what in human beings we call culture.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The bird that brought the species to public attention was a captive female named Betty, kept in a laboratory at Oxford. In 2002, researchers gave her and a male companion a choice between a straight piece of wire and a hooked one, to see which they would use to lift a small bucket of meat out of a tube. The male flew off with the hooked wire. Betty, left with the straight one, tried it without success, then wedged one end in a crack and pulled until the wire bent into a hook, and retrieved the food. She repeated the feat on nine of the next ten occasions. She had never seen wire before.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: At the time, Betty's behaviour was hailed as evidence of insight, the ability to picture a solution before carrying it out. Later fieldwork has made that interpretation less certain. Wild New Caledonian crows, it turns out, routinely bend twigs in exactly this way when making their tools, so that Betty may have been applying a natural habit to a new material and not inventing a technique from nothing. The finding is hardly less impressive, but it is a reminder of how easily a single striking observation can be over-interpreted.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Subsequent experiments have tested the birds more rigorously. In one, a crow had to use a short stick to pull a longer stick out of a box, and then use the longer one to reach food, a sequence of steps that requires holding a goal in mind. Most of the birds tested succeeded at the first attempt. In another, crows were shown a tube of water with a piece of food floating out of reach, and dropped stones into it to raise the level, choosing large stones over small ones and solid objects over hollow ones that would float. Children do not reliably solve this problem until they are about seven.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: How does a bird with a brain the size of a walnut manage it? Part of the answer is that size is misleading. The nerve cells in the forebrains of crows and parrots are much smaller and more tightly packed than those of mammals, so that a crow has as many of them in the relevant region as some monkeys. The other part is the way of life. Like apes, crows live long, grow up slowly and inhabit a complicated social world. New Caledonia also has no woodpeckers and few predators, which left a source of food unexploited and gave the crows the safety to spend time experimenting on the ground.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most significant lesson is about evolution. The last common ancestor of birds and mammals lived more than three hundred million years ago and was certainly no genius. The mental abilities of crows and of apes must therefore have arisen separately, in brains built on quite different plans. Intelligence, it seems, is not a single lucky accident on the branch of the family tree that leads to us. Given the right pressures, it can evolve more than once.

passage.title: The fire that remade a city

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early hours of Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in the bakery of Thomas Farriner in Pudding Lane, close to London Bridge. Fires were common in the city, and when the Lord Mayor was woken and brought to look at it, he was unimpressed and went back to bed. By the time it burned itself out four days later, it had destroyed more than thirteen thousand houses, eighty-seven churches and the medieval cathedral of St Paul's. Something like four fifths of the area within the city walls lay in ashes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: London had been a disaster waiting to happen. Its houses were built largely of timber, with upper storeys that jutted out over narrow lanes until they almost touched those opposite. Many roofs were thatched, in defiance of regulations that had forbidden thatch for centuries. Warehouses along the river were packed with oil, tar, spirits and timber. The summer of 1666 had been exceptionally hot and dry, and on the night the fire began a strong wind was blowing from the east, driving the flames towards the heart of the city.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The methods available for fighting it were primitive. There was no fire service. Each parish kept leather buckets, axes and long hooks, and the water supply ran through wooden pipes that had to be dug up and broken open. The only effective technique was to pull down houses in the path of the flames to create a gap. The Lord Mayor hesitated to order this, since the law made him liable for the cost of rebuilding any house destroyed on his instructions. By the time the king overruled him, the fire had grown too fierce to approach. It was finally halted on the Wednesday, when the wind dropped and sailors from the royal dockyards used gunpowder to blow up whole rows of houses.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Remarkably few deaths were recorded, fewer than ten according to the official figures, though some historians suspect the true number was higher, since the poor were not always counted and the heat was intense enough to leave no remains. The human cost lay elsewhere. Around seventy thousand people were made homeless and camped for months in the fields to the north. In the search for someone to blame, mobs attacked foreigners, and a French watchmaker who confessed to starting the fire was hanged, although it later emerged that he had not arrived in the country until after it began.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Within days, several ambitious plans for a new city had been laid before the king. The most famous was by Christopher Wren, who proposed sweeping away the tangle of medieval lanes in favour of broad, straight avenues meeting at open squares, in the manner of Paris or Rome. None of the plans was adopted. Thousands of owners held rights over small plots of land, and sorting out their claims in order to redraw the map would have taken years, while merchants were anxious to resume trading before their business moved elsewhere. Houses went up again along the old lines, and the street plan of the City of London today is still, in essentials, the medieval one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If the layout stayed the same, the buildings did not. An Act of Parliament passed in 1667 laid down rules that transformed the appearance of the city. All new houses were to be of brick or stone. Their height was fixed according to the width of the street, in four classes. Upper floors could no longer project, and the principal streets were widened. Surveyors were appointed to inspect the work. These were among the first comprehensive building regulations in Europe, and they were paid for by a tax on the coal brought into London by sea.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The fire had less obvious consequences as well. Disputes between landlords and tenants over who should pay for rebuilding were so numerous that a special court was created to settle them quickly, and it sat for nine years. A physician turned speculative builder, Nicholas Barbon, saw a commercial opportunity and in 1680 set up an office that, in return for an annual payment, undertook to rebuild a client's house if it burned. He also employed his own teams of men to put fires out, and marked the houses he insured with a metal badge. This was the beginning of the fire insurance industry, and, since the insurers' brigades were for more than a century the only organised firefighters in London, of the fire service too.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One popular belief about the fire deserves a brief mention. It is often said that the flames ended the Great Plague, which had killed perhaps a fifth of London's population the year before, by destroying the rats and the filthy housing that harboured it. The timing makes this unlikely. The epidemic was already fading before the fire, and the districts where it had been worst were the poor suburbs outside the walls, which the flames never reached.
