paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Almost everyone delays tasks from time to time. For a substantial minority, estimated at around a fifth of adults, the habit is persistent and damaging. They pay bills late, put off visits to the doctor, and submit work at the last minute or not at all. Surveys of university students suggest that most of them regard procrastination as a problem, and it has been linked with lower marks, poorer health and reduced earnings. The puzzling feature of the behaviour is that people do it knowingly. To procrastinate is not simply to postpone, which may be perfectly sensible. It is to postpone something while expecting to be worse off as a result.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The usual explanation, offered by procrastinators themselves as readily as by their critics, is poor time management or plain laziness. Neither stands up well. Procrastinators are often busy, tidying their desks or answering unimportant messages, while the dreaded task waits. And courses that teach planning and scheduling have a disappointing record. They help people who are disorganised, but they do little for those who know exactly what they should be doing and still do not do it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Economists have approached the problem through the way people value the future. Offered a choice between a sum of money in a year and a slightly larger sum in a year and a day, nearly everyone is content to wait the extra day. Offered the same choice between today and tomorrow, many take the smaller sum at once. A reward that is immediate looms disproportionately large. The same is true of costs. The effort of starting a report is felt now, while the benefit of finishing it lies weeks away, and so the balance tips towards delay. The trouble is that when tomorrow arrives, it has become today, and the same reasoning applies again.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Psychologists have added an emotional dimension. In their account, procrastination is less a failure to manage time than a failure to manage mood. A task that provokes anxiety, boredom or self-doubt is unpleasant to think about, and avoiding it brings instant relief. That relief is a reward, and behaviour that is rewarded tends to be repeated. The cost comes later, in guilt and in the stress of a looming deadline, which make the task more unpleasant still and the urge to escape it stronger. Brain imaging studies offer some support, having found that habitual procrastinators show differences in regions involved in regulating emotion.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This helps to explain a finding that surprises many people. It might be expected that those who are hardest on themselves would be the least likely to delay. The reverse appears to be true. In a study of students preparing for examinations, those who forgave themselves for having procrastinated before the first test procrastinated less before the second. Harsh self-criticism seems to add to the negative feelings that drive avoidance, whereas treating a lapse with some kindness makes it easier to face the task again.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A fascinating series of experiments suggests that part of the problem lies in how we think about our future selves. When people are asked to imagine themselves ten years from now while their brains are scanned, the pattern of activity resembles that produced by thinking about a stranger more than that produced by thinking about themselves. If the person who will suffer from our delay feels like someone else, it is not surprising that we are willing to hand them the burden. In one study, volunteers who were shown digitally aged photographs of their own faces subsequently chose to put more money into a savings account for retirement.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What, then, actually helps? The evidence favours methods that reduce the emotional cost of beginning. One is to shrink the first step until it no longer provokes resistance, committing oneself only to write a single sentence or to work for five minutes. Starting is usually the hardest part, and once under way most people continue. Another is to decide in advance exactly when and where a task will be done, in the form of a specific plan. A third is to remove temptations beforehand, on the principle that it is easier to avoid a distraction than to resist it. Deadlines imposed by someone else are more effective than those we set ourselves. In a well-known experiment, students who were given three evenly spaced deadlines for three essays did better than those who were allowed to hand in all three at the end of term, and also better than those who chose their own dates.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It is worth adding that not every delay is a vice. Some writers have praised what they call structured procrastination, in which a person avoids one task by completing others that are useful. And there is evidence that leaving a creative problem unfinished for a while can improve the eventual solution, since the mind continues to work on it in the background. The difficulty, as always, lies in telling a productive pause from an excuse.

passage.title: When the desert was a grassland

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the heart of the Sahara, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest permanent water, there are cliffs covered with paintings and carvings. They show giraffes, elephants and hippopotamuses, herds of cattle, and in one remote cave a row of small human figures that appear to be swimming. Bones of crocodiles and fish hooks carved from bone have been dug from the sand nearby. The people who made these images were not imagining another country. They were recording the world around them. Between roughly eleven thousand and five thousand years ago, the largest hot desert on earth was a land of lakes, rivers and grass.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The cause lay far away, in the motion of the earth itself. The planet's axis is not fixed but wobbles slowly, like a spinning top, completing a circle about every twenty-three thousand years. The effect is to change the season in which each hemisphere is closest to the sun. Eleven thousand years ago, the northern summer coincided with the earth's nearest approach, so that summers in North Africa received noticeably more sunlight than they do now. The land heated more strongly, the air above it rose, and moist air was drawn in from the Atlantic to replace it. The belt of summer rain that today barely reaches the southern fringe of the desert moved a thousand kilometres to the north.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The change in sunlight alone, however, was too small to account for the transformation. Climate models that included nothing else could not make the Sahara green enough to match the evidence. The missing element was the land's own response. Bare sand is pale and reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it. Grass and shrubs are darker, absorb more heat, and return water to the air through their leaves. Once plants began to spread, they warmed and moistened the air above them, which strengthened the rains, which allowed more plants to grow. A modest push from the sun was magnified by the vegetation into a new climate.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The evidence for that climate is abundant. Radar images taken from space reveal the channels of great rivers buried under the dunes. Lake Chad, which today is shallow and shrinking, was then an inland sea larger than any lake on earth now, and its ancient shoreline can still be traced. Cores of mud drilled from the floor of the Atlantic, off the coast of West Africa, provide a continuous record. In the layers laid down during the humid period, there is far less of the dust that winds now carry out from the desert, and far more of the chemical traces left by leafy plants.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How the wet period ended has been a matter of dispute. The slow change in the earth's orbit that had brought the rains gradually took them away again, over several thousand years. Yet the ocean cores off the north-west coast appear to show the supply of dust rising sharply within a few centuries, about five and a half thousand years ago, as though the system had flipped. Records from lakes further east tell a different story, of a decline spread over millennia. The likeliest explanation is that both are right, and that the drying was sudden in some regions and slow in others, depending on local conditions.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have suggested that people played a part. By this time the inhabitants were herding cattle, sheep and goats, and heavy grazing may have stripped away vegetation in areas that were already under stress, hastening the return of bare ground. Others argue the opposite, that herders, by moving their animals with the seasons, would have helped to keep the grassland in balance, and that the collapse came from the climate alone. The question is unresolved.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: What is not in doubt is the effect on the people. As the grassland failed, they moved towards the few places where water remained, above all the valley of the Nile. It is surely no coincidence that the first settled kingdoms of Egypt arose in the centuries after the Sahara dried, when a growing population was crowded into a narrow strip of fertile land and had to organise itself to share it.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The cycle continues, and in the ordinary course of things the Sahara would turn green again in ten thousand years or so. Whether human influence on the climate will alter that timetable is unknown. Some models suggest that a warmer world will bring more rain to the southern edge of the desert, and satellite images over recent decades do show parts of that zone becoming greener. But the lesson of the past is one of caution. It shows that the desert's border is not fixed, and that a small change can be amplified by the land into a very large one, in either direction.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every winter since 1900, on a single day around Christmas, volunteers across North America have gone out to count the birds they can see within a set area. The custom was begun by an ornithologist who wanted to replace a traditional holiday hunt with something less destructive. More than a century later, the count involves tens of thousands of people, and its records form the longest continuous survey of wildlife in existence. Scientists have used them to show how the ranges of hundreds of species have shifted northwards as winters have warmed. No team of professionals could have gathered such data, and no research budget could have paid for it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The participation of amateurs in research is not new. Until the late nineteenth century, most science was done by people who were not paid for it, and Charles Darwin himself held no university post. What has changed is the scale, and the cause is technology. A smartphone can record a photograph, the time and an exact location, and transmit all three in seconds. On one popular platform, users upload pictures of plants and animals, software suggests an identification, and other users confirm or correct it. The platform has accumulated well over a hundred million records, among them species previously unknown to science and others that had been presumed extinct.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second kind of project needs no fieldwork at all. Modern instruments produce more data than scientists can examine. In 2007, astronomers at Oxford, faced with images of a million galaxies that had to be sorted by shape, put them on a website and invited the public to help. They expected the task to take years. Within twenty-four hours, visitors were classifying fifty thousand images an hour. Because each galaxy was shown to many people, mistakes by individuals were outvoted, and the combined result proved as reliable as the judgment of experts. One participant, a Dutch schoolteacher, noticed a strange green object that fitted none of the categories. It turned out to be a kind of gas cloud that nobody had seen before, and it now bears her name.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A third approach turns research into a game. Working out how a protein folds into its three-dimensional shape is a notoriously hard problem, and one at which people's intuition about space can outperform a computer's calculation. Biochemists in Seattle designed a puzzle in which players twist and tuck a protein on screen and earn points for more stable arrangements. In 2011, players of this game determined the structure of an enzyme from a virus related to HIV in three weeks, a problem that had defeated researchers for fifteen years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The obvious objection is that data collected by untrained people cannot be trusted. Studies that have checked suggest that the concern is real but manageable. Volunteers tend to be good at spotting common, distinctive species and poor at rare or similar-looking ones. They visit attractive places at weekends in fine weather, so that records are thin for remote areas, weekdays and winter. Well-designed projects allow for this, by providing training, by asking several volunteers to examine the same item, and by using statistical methods that correct for uneven effort. Where these safeguards are in place, comparisons have generally found the quality of amateur data to be close to that of professionals.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There are deeper questions about who takes part and who benefits. Surveys indicate that volunteers are far from representative of the population. They tend to be older, wealthier and more highly educated than average. And the relationship can be one-sided. Volunteers supply their time and observations, while the questions are set, and the papers written, by academics. Critics have asked whether such arrangements deserve to be called participation at all, and some projects have been accused of using the public as free labour.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A different model has emerged in response, in which communities decide for themselves what needs investigating. Residents of a district near an oil refinery in the United States, worried about their health and dissatisfied with official monitoring, learned to take air samples with simple equipment made from plastic buckets. Their results revealed levels of pollution that the authorities' instruments had missed, and eventually forced stricter controls. After the nuclear accident at Fukushima in Japan in 2011, volunteers who distrusted official figures built their own radiation detectors, fixed them to cars, and produced a public map more detailed than the government's.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Enthusiasts sometimes claim that citizen science will transform the relationship between researchers and society. That may be too much to expect. Most volunteers contribute once or twice and are never heard from again, and a small core does the bulk of the work. But there is good evidence that taking part improves people's understanding of how science operates, including its uncertainties. At a time when trust in expertise cannot be taken for granted, that may prove to be as valuable as the data.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the normal way to earn a living in industrial countries was to hold a job. A worker was hired by an employer, turned up at fixed hours, and in return received a wage, paid holidays, sick pay and, eventually, a pension. Over the past fifteen years, a different arrangement has spread, in which people are paid not for their time but for each task they complete, whether a car journey, a meal delivered or a piece of translation. The tasks are distributed by software, usually through an app on a phone. This has become known as the gig economy, a term borrowed from musicians, who have always been paid by the performance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its growth has been rapid, though measuring it is harder than might be supposed. Official statistics were designed for a world of employees and the self-employed, and people who do a few hours of app-based work alongside a regular job are easily missed. Surveys in Europe and North America suggest that between one in twenty and one in ten adults does some work of this kind in a given year, but that only a small fraction rely on it for most of their income. For the majority, it is a supplement.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The companies that run the platforms describe themselves not as employers but as marketplaces that bring customers and independent workers together. The distinction matters a great deal. Someone who is classed as an independent contractor has no right to a minimum wage, to paid leave or to compensation if dismissed, and the company pays no contributions towards their health care or retirement. In exchange, it is argued, the worker enjoys freedom. There is no boss, no shift pattern and no obligation to accept any particular task.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Surveys of workers lend some support to this picture. Asked what they value most, a large majority mention flexibility. Students, parents of young children and people caring for elderly relatives can fit paid work around their other commitments in a way that few conventional jobs allow. For those shut out of ordinary employment, because of a gap in their record or a lack of qualifications, platform work offers an income with almost no barrier to entry.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Critics reply that the freedom is more apparent than real. A driver may choose when to log in, but once logged in, the app decides which jobs are offered and at what price, and it monitors the driver's speed, route and rate of acceptance. Those who decline too many requests may find that fewer are offered, or that their account is suspended, often without explanation or appeal. The role of manager has not disappeared. It has been taken over by a set of rules that the worker cannot see and cannot question. Researchers have also drawn attention to earnings. When the cost of fuel, insurance and wear on a vehicle is subtracted, and the unpaid time spent waiting for work is counted, the hourly income of many drivers falls close to, or below, the legal minimum for employees.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The question of status has been fought out in the courts of many countries, with varying results. In 2021, the highest court in Britain ruled that drivers for one of the largest ride-hailing firms were not independent contractors but workers, a category in British law that carries the right to the minimum wage and holiday pay. The judges observed that the company set the fares, dictated the terms and controlled the drivers' performance through ratings, and that it was hard to see what business the drivers were supposedly running on their own account. In California, by contrast, voters approved a measure, heavily funded by the platforms themselves, that kept drivers as contractors while granting them a limited set of benefits.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Some economists believe the debate has been framed too narrowly, as a choice between two categories devised a century ago. They propose a third status, with protections that are attached to the individual and not to the job. Under such a scheme, every platform for which a person worked would pay a small percentage of their earnings into a personal account, which could be drawn on for sickness, holidays or retirement. Experiments along these lines are under way in several places, though trade unions tend to regard them with suspicion, fearing that employers of all kinds would use an intermediate category to reduce the rights of existing staff.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It is worth noting, finally, that the arrangement is not as new as it seems. In nineteenth-century ports, dockworkers gathered at the gates each morning in the hope of being picked for a day's labour, and in the cloth trade, weavers were paid by the piece for work done at home. Regular employment with its attached protections was a later invention, won over decades. Seen in that light, the gig economy is less a product of technology than the return of a much older pattern, and the question it raises is the old one of how the risks of working life should be shared.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Along cold, rocky coasts from Norway to New Zealand grow forests that few people ever see. They are made not of trees but of kelp, a group of large brown seaweeds. A kelp has no roots. It grips the rock with a tangle of finger-like growths, and from this base a flexible stalk rises towards the surface, bearing long blades that are held up in some species by gas-filled floats. The largest, the giant kelp of the Pacific, can reach forty-five metres and may grow half a metre in a single day, faster than almost any other living thing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Like a forest on land, a kelp forest has layers. The blades at the surface form a canopy that shades the water below. Beneath it, smaller seaweeds make up an understorey, and the sea floor is carpeted with sponges, anemones and encrusting algae. This structure provides food and shelter for an extraordinary variety of animals. Young fish hide among the blades. Snails and crabs graze on them. Seals and sea lions hunt in the shadows, and sea otters wrap themselves in the floating fronds before sleeping, so as not to drift away.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The forests matter to people as well. They slow the waves that strike the shore, reducing erosion. They are nurseries for species on which commercial fisheries depend. Substances extracted from kelp are used to thicken ice cream, toothpaste and many other products. And because kelp grows so fast, it absorbs large amounts of carbon dioxide. How much of that carbon is locked away for the long term is still debated. Unlike a tree, kelp does not store carbon in wood or soil. Some pieces break off and sink into the deep ocean, where the carbon may remain for centuries, but much of the plant is eaten or decays and returns its carbon to the water.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For all their vigour, kelp forests can vanish with astonishing speed. The classic case comes from the Pacific coast of North America. Sea urchins, spiny animals the size of a tennis ball, feed on kelp. In a healthy forest they stay hidden in crevices and eat fragments that drift down. Their numbers are held in check by predators, the most important of which is the sea otter. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur. Freed from control, urchins multiplied, came out into the open, and chewed through the bases of the kelp. What remained was bare rock covered with urchins, a condition known as an urchin barren.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Where otters were later protected and returned, the kelp generally came back, and the story became a textbook example of how the loss of a single predator can transform an ecosystem. It has, however, proved to be only part of the picture. In northern California, more than nine tenths of the kelp disappeared between 2014 and 2019, although there had been no otters on that stretch of coast for well over a century. The cause was a combination of events. A disease wiped out a large starfish that also eats urchins. At the same time, a prolonged marine heatwave weakened the kelp, which needs cold, nutrient-rich water. The urchins, with no predators left and a struggling forest before them, did the rest.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Warming seas are now the greatest threat. Kelp forests have retreated along the coasts of Western Australia, Tasmania, Japan and southern Europe, in some places replaced by low, turf-like algae that support far less life. A barren, once established, is difficult to reverse. Urchins can survive for years on almost nothing, shrinking their bodies and waiting, and they consume any young kelp that tries to settle. Simply removing the original cause is therefore not enough to bring the forest back.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Efforts at restoration take several forms. In California and Norway, divers have been employed to remove or crush urchins by hand, which works on a small scale but is slow and costly. A Norwegian company has experimented with collecting the starved urchins from barrens and fattening them in tanks for sale as a delicacy, in the hope of turning a pest into a product. In Australia, scientists have identified individual kelp plants that tolerate warmer water and are breeding from them for replanting. And in South Korea and Japan, where seaweed has long been farmed for food, artificial reefs seeded with kelp have been laid over large areas.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: There is growing interest, too, in farming kelp in the open sea, for food, for animal feed and as a way of capturing carbon. Supporters point out that it needs no land, fresh water or fertiliser. Sceptics caution that the quantities required to make any difference to the climate would be immense, and that the effects of sinking vast amounts of seaweed into the deep ocean are unknown. What is not in doubt is that the natural forests are worth far more standing than lost, and that protecting those which remain is cheaper than trying to rebuild them.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ask most people how money began, and they will tell a story that goes something like this. Once, people exchanged goods directly. A farmer with grain to spare would look for a potter who wanted grain and had pots to offer. This was inconvenient, since each had to want exactly what the other possessed. So people settled on a single commodity, such as salt, shells or eventually gold, that everyone would accept, and money was born. The account appears in the opening chapters of countless economics textbooks, and it can be traced back to the eighteenth-century philosopher Adam Smith.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that there is almost no evidence that it ever happened. Anthropologists who have studied societies without money have looked hard for economies based on barter and have not found them. The Cambridge anthropologist Caroline Humphrey, who reviewed the research in the 1980s, concluded that no example of a pure barter economy had ever been described, let alone one from which money emerged. Barter certainly occurs, but typically between strangers or enemies who do not expect to meet again, or among people who are used to money and find themselves without it, such as prisoners.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: How, then, did people in small communities obtain what they needed from one another? The answer suggested by the evidence is that they did so on credit. If a neighbour needed a pot, the potter gave him one, and it was understood that something was owed in return, at some later time and in some other form. Everyone in a village knew, roughly, who owed what to whom. Such obligations were not precisely measured, and that was part of their purpose, since a debt that is never quite settled keeps a relationship alive. On this view, money did not replace barter. It grew out of the attempt to put numbers on debts.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The earliest written records support the idea. In the cities of Mesopotamia five thousand years ago, the temples and palaces that ran much of the economy kept detailed accounts on clay tablets. They recorded rents, loans and rations in terms of standard units, a weight of silver and a measure of barley that were treated as equivalent. Yet silver seldom changed hands. It sat in the treasuries, while ordinary people paid what they owed in barley, wool or labour at harvest time. Money existed as a way of reckoning long before it existed as an object in the pocket.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The first true coins were struck much later, around 600 BC, in the kingdom of Lydia in what is now western Turkey. They were lumps of a natural mixture of gold and silver, stamped with the image of a lion to guarantee their weight. Within a couple of centuries the practice had spread across the Greek world, and coins appeared independently in India and China at about the same period. Why then, and why in those places? One influential answer links coins to war. A ruler who needed to pay and feed a large army far from home could hardly do so in promises. He paid the soldiers in stamped metal, and then demanded that his subjects pay their taxes in the same metal. The population was thus obliged to supply the soldiers with food and goods in order to obtain the coins they needed, and markets grew up wherever armies went.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The contrast between the two forms of money, credit and coin, runs through later history. Credit depends on trust and works well within a community where people know one another and expect to deal again. Coin requires no trust at all, which is why it is favoured in dealings with strangers, and why it flourishes in times of violence, when it can be stolen as easily as spent. Some historians see a long alternation between the two. Periods dominated by great empires and their armies were ages of coin. After the fall of Rome, coins largely vanished from Europe, yet trade did not stop. Accounts were kept, in the old imperial units, by monasteries and merchants, and debts were settled at periodic fairs with very little metal changing hands.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Seen in this way, the present is less of a departure than it appears. Most of the money in a modern economy has no physical existence. It consists of entries in the records of banks, created when a loan is made and cancelled when it is repaid. Payment by card or phone has made coins and notes rarer still. We tend to think of this as a recent and rather abstract development. It may be better understood as a return to what money was in the beginning, a system for keeping track of what people owe one another.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the annual World Memory Championships, competitors perform feats that seem to belong to science fiction. They memorise the order of a shuffled pack of cards in under twenty seconds, or recite a thousand random digits after studying them for an hour. It would be natural to assume that these people were born with exceptional minds. They insist that they were not, and research supports them. What they have is a technique, and it is one of the oldest known.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its invention is credited, in a story told by the Roman writer Cicero, to a Greek poet named Simonides, who lived about two and a half thousand years ago. Simonides was performing at a banquet when he was called outside. While he was gone, the roof of the hall collapsed, crushing the other guests so badly that their relatives could not tell the bodies apart. Simonides found that he could identify each one by recalling where it had been sitting. From this he drew a general principle. The mind remembers places and images far more easily than words or numbers, so the way to remember anything is to convert it into images and arrange them in a place.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The method that grew from this insight is known as the memory palace. The first step is to choose a building or a route that one knows intimately, such as one's own home or the walk to work. The second is to turn each item to be remembered into a vivid picture, the more absurd, comic or shocking the better, since ordinary things are easily forgotten. The third is to place the pictures, one by one, at fixed points along the route, by the front door, on the stairs, in the bath. To recall the list, one simply takes the walk again in imagination and observes what is there.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For the orators of Greece and Rome, who spoke for hours without notes, the technique was a standard part of education. In the Middle Ages, when books were rare and costly, scholars and preachers used it to store entire texts, and treated a trained memory as a mark of character as much as of intellect. The art declined after the invention of printing made it less necessary, and by the twentieth century it survived mainly among stage performers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Scientific interest revived when psychologists began to study the champions. Brain scans showed nothing unusual in the structure of their brains, and on tests of general ability they scored no higher than other people. What distinguished them was which regions were active while they memorised. In addition to the areas everyone uses, they recruited those involved in spatial navigation, the same regions that are enlarged in London taxi drivers, who must learn the layout of twenty-five thousand streets.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The decisive experiment was published in 2017 by a team in the Netherlands. They recruited volunteers with ordinary memories and gave one group half an hour of daily training in the memory palace for six weeks. A second group practised a different kind of memory exercise, and a third did nothing. At the start, the volunteers could recall on average about twenty-six words from a list of seventy-two. After training, the memory palace group recalled sixty-two, and four months later, without further practice, they could still manage nearly fifty. The other groups improved only slightly. Moreover, scans showed that the patterns of connection in the trained volunteers' brains had come to resemble those of the champions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If the technique is so powerful, why is it not taught in every school? Part of the answer is that it has limits. It is well suited to lists, sequences and facts that have no inner logic, such as vocabulary, dates or the bones of the hand. It is of little help with material that has to be understood, where the connections between ideas matter more than the ideas in isolation. A student who memorised a physics textbook by this method would be able to recite it and still be unable to solve a problem. It also demands effort. Composing images takes time, and for a shopping list most people reasonably prefer a piece of paper.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: There is a further point, which the champions themselves often make. The method works because it forces the learner to pay attention, to do something active and inventive with each item instead of reading it passively and hoping it will stay. That, more than the palace itself, may be its lasting lesson. Several competitors have remarked that outside the hall their memories are as unreliable as anyone's, and that they still lose their keys.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a market in northern Thailand, stalls are piled with fried crickets, bamboo worms and giant water bugs, and customers buy them by the bag as a snack. In Mexico, grasshoppers toasted with lime and chilli have been eaten since before the Spanish arrived. In southern Africa, the caterpillar of the emperor moth is dried and sold in quantities worth tens of millions of dollars a year. Around two billion people, in more than a hundred countries, eat insects as an ordinary part of their diet. It is the inhabitants of Europe and North America, who do not, that are the exception.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In 2013, a report from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations argued that the rest of the world should take the habit seriously. The global population is expected to approach ten billion by the middle of the century, and demand for animal protein is rising faster still as incomes grow. Meeting it by conventional means would require far more land, water and feed than the planet can easily supply. Insects, the report suggested, could provide part of the answer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The nutritional case is strong. Weight for weight, dried crickets contain more protein than beef, along with iron, zinc and several vitamins. The fats in many edible insects are of the kind considered healthy. They also contain fibre, in the form of chitin, the material of their outer shells, which meat lacks altogether. The quality varies considerably between species and according to what the insects themselves have been fed, but in general they compare well with other animal foods.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The environmental case rests on efficiency. Insects are cold-blooded and do not burn energy to keep their bodies warm, so more of what they eat is turned into growth. To produce a kilogram of weight, crickets need roughly two kilograms of feed, whereas cattle need about eight. Moreover, around eighty per cent of a cricket can be eaten, compared with less than half of a cow. Insects require a fraction of the water and space, can be reared in stacked trays in a warehouse, and release far smaller quantities of greenhouse gases. Certain species offer a further advantage. The larvae of the black soldier fly will feed on almost any organic waste, including vegetable peelings, spent grain from breweries and manure, converting material that would otherwise be thrown away into protein.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: These claims come with qualifications. Most of the favourable figures are derived from small trials, and it is uncertain whether they will hold at industrial scale. Insects reared on waste grow more slowly and less reliably than those given high-quality grain, and if they are fed on grain, part of the environmental advantage disappears, since the grain could have been eaten by people directly. Insects reared in cool climates need heated buildings, which consume energy. One study that tried to account for all of this found that crickets fed on poultry feed were no more efficient than chickens. The benefit is real, but it depends heavily on how the farming is done.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Safety raises questions as well. People who are allergic to shellfish may react to insects, which are distant relatives of shrimps and crabs. Insects gathered from the wild can carry pesticides or heavy metals. And farming animals in dense colonies always carries a risk of disease, though no infection of insects is known to pass to humans. Regulators have moved cautiously. The European Union approved its first insect, the yellow mealworm, as food only in 2021.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The largest obstacle in Western countries is not safety but disgust. The reaction is learned and not innate, as is shown by the fact that the same consumers happily eat prawns, lobsters and snails, and regard honey, which is produced inside the body of a bee, as wholesome. Yet a learned reaction can be extremely stubborn. Experiments suggest that people are more willing to try insects when they cannot see them. Cricket flour baked into bread or protein bars is accepted far more readily than a whole roasted cricket, and several companies have built their business on that finding. The history of other foods offers some encouragement. Raw fish was regarded with horror in the United States in the 1960s and is now sold as sushi in every supermarket, and the lobster was once considered fit only for prisoners and the poor.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: For the present, the most promising use of insects may be one that avoids the problem of taste entirely. Much of the world's farmed fish and poultry is fed on meal made from soya or from wild fish caught for the purpose, both of which carry heavy environmental costs. Insect larvae are a natural food for chickens and fish, and trials have shown that they can replace a substantial part of the conventional feed without affecting growth. In this roundabout way, a good many people who would never knowingly eat an insect may soon be doing so at one remove.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For four centuries after Europeans first crossed the narrow strip of land joining North and South America, people dreamed of cutting a channel through it. A ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to travel some twenty thousand kilometres round the southern tip of South America, a voyage of months through some of the roughest seas in the world. A canal across the isthmus of Panama, only eighty kilometres wide, would shorten the journey by more than half.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first serious attempt was made by the French, and it was led by the most celebrated engineer of the age. Ferdinand de Lesseps had completed the Suez Canal in 1869 and was regarded as a national hero. He proposed to repeat the achievement in Panama, digging a channel at sea level from one ocean to the other. Work began in 1881. But Suez had been a ditch through flat, dry desert. Panama was mountainous jungle with one of the heaviest rainfalls on earth. The river that crossed the route could rise ten metres in a day, and the hillsides, once cut into, slid back into the excavation almost as fast as they were dug.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The greater enemy was disease. Yellow fever and malaria killed the workers in their thousands, and nobody knew how they were transmitted. The French hospitals, in an effort to keep ants from climbing into patients' beds, stood the legs of the beds in dishes of water, and so provided ideal breeding places for the mosquitoes that carried the infections. By the time the company collapsed in bankruptcy in 1889, it is thought that more than twenty thousand people had died. Hundreds of thousands of small investors in France lost their savings, and the scandal that followed brought down a government.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The United States took over the project in 1904, having first encouraged the province of Panama to break away from Colombia and then signed a treaty with the new country that gave it control of a strip of land on either side of the route. The Americans made two decisions that the French had not. The first concerned health. By this time it had been shown that mosquitoes spread both diseases, and the army doctor William Gorgas set about destroying them. His teams drained swamps, covered water tanks, fitted screens to windows and sprayed standing water with oil. Yellow fever was eliminated from the canal zone within two years, and malaria was greatly reduced.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The second decision concerned the design. The chief engineer, John Stevens, concluded that a sea-level canal was impossible and persuaded the government to build a canal with locks. The river would be dammed to create an enormous artificial lake, twenty-six metres above the sea. Ships would be raised to the lake by a flight of three locks, sail across it, pass through a deep cutting in the mountains, and be lowered by three more locks on the far side. The water to fill the locks would flow from the lake by gravity, so that no pumps were needed. Stevens, a railwayman by training, also saw that the essential problem was not digging but removing what had been dug, and he laid out a system of tracks on which trains carried the spoil away in a continuous procession.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The canal opened in August 1914, six months ahead of schedule and under budget, though the occasion was overshadowed by the outbreak of war in Europe that same month. Some fifty-six thousand people had worked on it under the Americans, the majority of them labourers recruited from the islands of the Caribbean. They were paid far less than white American employees, housed separately, and given the most dangerous work, and it was among them that most of the five thousand or so deaths of the American period occurred.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The canal transformed world trade, and it remained under American control for most of the century. That arrangement was increasingly resented in Panama, and after years of negotiation the waterway was handed over to the Panamanian government on the last day of 1999. A third, larger set of locks was opened in 2016 to take the much bigger ships now in service.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The canal's future is less secure than its past. Each ship that passes through releases about two hundred million litres of fresh water from the lake into the sea, and that water has to be replaced by rain. In 2023, a severe drought lowered the lake so far that the authorities were forced to cut the number of daily crossings by more than a third, and ships queued for weeks at either end. The same lake supplies drinking water to half the country's population. A structure that was designed to conquer geography turns out to depend, in the end, on the weather.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A supermarket in a wealthy country may stock forty thousand different products, including dozens of kinds of olive oil and hundreds of breakfast cereals. Economic theory has traditionally treated this as an unmixed blessing. The more options there are, the more likely it is that each customer will find one that exactly matches his or her tastes, and anyone who dislikes the abundance is free to ignore it. Around the turn of the century, a group of psychologists began to argue that this view was mistaken, and that beyond a certain point, extra choice makes people less likely to choose anything and less happy with what they choose.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The experiment that launched the idea was carried out in a food shop in California by Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper. On some days, they set up a table offering samples of twenty-four varieties of jam. On other days, the table held only six. The large display attracted more shoppers, sixty per cent of those who passed, compared with forty per cent for the small one. But when it came to buying, the pattern was reversed. Of those who stopped at the table of six, nearly a third went on to buy a jar. Of those who stopped at the table of twenty-four, only three per cent did.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The psychologist Barry Schwartz developed the finding into a general theory, which he called the paradox of choice. A large number of options, he suggested, burdens the chooser in several ways. Comparing them takes effort, and some people abandon the attempt. The more alternatives are rejected, the easier it is to imagine that one of them would have been better, so that regret increases. Expectations rise too. With only two styles of jeans on offer, a poor fit is the manufacturer's fault. With two hundred, there seems no excuse for not finding the perfect pair, and the buyer who is still not satisfied has no one to blame but himself.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Schwartz drew a distinction between two kinds of people. Maximisers feel that they must find the best possible option, and so examine every alternative. Satisficers look only until they find something good enough and then stop. In his surveys, maximisers tended to obtain objectively better results, for instance higher starting salaries after university. They were nevertheless less content with the outcome, and more prone to regret and to comparing themselves with others.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The theory was enormously influential. Companies reduced their product ranges, and one manufacturer reported that sales of a brand of shampoo rose by a tenth after the number of versions was cut from twenty-six to fifteen. Governments took note as well. When Sweden reformed its pension system and invited citizens to select from more than four hundred investment funds, most made no active choice at all and were placed in the default.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Then came the doubts. Other researchers who tried to repeat the jam experiment obtained inconsistent results, and in 2010 a team led by Benjamin Scheibehenne combined the data from fifty published and unpublished studies. Taken together, they showed an average effect of almost exactly zero. In some experiments more choice reduced purchases, in others it increased them, and in most it made no difference. Choice overload, it seemed, was not a general law of human behaviour.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Later work has tried to establish when it does occur. A second, larger analysis identified several conditions under which too many options do appear to cause problems. One is when the options are hard to compare, because they differ in many ways at once. Another is when the chooser has no clear preference to begin with and knows little about the subject, as with pensions or medical treatments. A third is when the options are presented in a disorderly way. Sorting them into a few categories, or allowing people to filter by features that matter to them, largely removes the difficulty. An expert choosing wine from a long but well-organised list is in a quite different position from a novice facing a wall of bottles.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The episode has been instructive in more than one way. It is a reminder that a single vivid experiment, however appealing its message, is a weak foundation for sweeping conclusions. And it suggests that the useful question is not how many options people should be offered, but how. For decisions that are complicated and important, such as saving for retirement, a sensible default and a short, well-arranged menu serve people better than either a single compulsory option or a bewildering multitude.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Earthquakes cannot be predicted. Despite a century of effort and many false hopes, no one has found a reliable sign that a fault is about to slip, and most seismologists doubt that such a sign exists. What can be done, however, is to detect an earthquake in the first moments after it begins and to send a warning that outruns the shaking. In several countries, systems of this kind now give people between a few seconds and a minute to prepare. It does not sound like much. It can be enough to save lives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The method depends on a simple fact of physics. When a fault ruptures, it sends out waves of two main kinds. The first to arrive, known as primary waves, travel through rock at about six kilometres a second and compress the ground in the direction of travel. They are felt as a sharp jolt and seldom cause damage. Behind them come the secondary waves, which move at roughly half the speed and shake the ground from side to side. It is these, and the surface waves that follow, that bring buildings down. The further a place lies from the source, the longer the gap between the two.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An early warning system exploits this gap. A dense network of sensors is installed across a region. When several of those nearest the source register the first waves, computers estimate the location and size of the earthquake within a second or two and calculate which areas will be shaken and how strongly. An alert is then transmitted by radio, internet and mobile phone networks. Since such signals travel at close to the speed of light, they easily overtake the destructive waves.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The idea is older than might be imagined. In 1868, after an earthquake damaged San Francisco, a local doctor proposed in a newspaper that telegraph wires could carry a warning from sensors outside the city and ring a bell in its centre. Nothing came of it. The first working system was built in Japan in the 1960s to protect the new high-speed railway, cutting power to trains automatically when sensors along the coast detected strong motion. Mexico City followed in 1991, six years after an earthquake three hundred and fifty kilometres away on the Pacific coast had killed thousands of its inhabitants. Because the city lies so far from the faults that threaten it, it can receive more than a minute's warning.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Japan now operates the most advanced public system in the world. Alerts interrupt television and radio programmes and sound on every mobile phone in the affected area. Factories halt production lines, surgeons pause operations, lifts stop at the nearest floor and open their doors, and gas supplies shut off. When a great earthquake struck off the north-east coast in March 2011, the system issued its alert eight seconds after the first wave was detected, and people in Tokyo had about a minute before strong shaking arrived. Every one of the high-speed trains running in the region slowed and stopped without a single derailment.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The systems have limits that their operators are careful to explain. The most serious is the blind zone. Close to the source, the damaging waves arrive almost as soon as the first, before any alert can be issued, so that the people in greatest danger receive the least warning or none. In addition, the size of a very large earthquake cannot be known at the outset, because the rupture itself may take a minute or more to travel along the fault. In 2011 the Japanese system at first greatly underestimated the magnitude, and with it the height of the tsunami that followed. False alarms are a further concern. A system that cries wolf too often will be ignored, while one that is too cautious will miss real events.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The cost of sensor networks has put them beyond the reach of many countries at risk. A cheaper approach uses the instruments people already carry. Every smartphone contains a tiny device that detects motion, intended for turning the screen and counting steps. Software can recognise the characteristic signature of an earthquake, and when many phones in the same area report it at the same moment, a central computer can be confident that the event is real. A system of this kind has been operating on phones using one common operating system since 2020, and it has issued alerts in countries from Greece to the Philippines that have no network of their own.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: A warning is useful only if people know what to do with it. Studies of those who received alerts suggest that many simply wait to see what happens, or try to run outside, which is more dangerous than staying put. Education matters as much as engineering. In Japan, where children practise from their first year at school, the response is close to automatic, which is to drop to the floor, take cover under a table and hold on.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, surgery was a last resort, and for good reason. Patients were fully conscious. They were held down by strong assistants or strapped to the table, sometimes after a dose of alcohol or opium that did little to dull the agony. The most admired surgeons were the fastest. Robert Liston of London could remove a leg in under a minute, and the pain and shock were such that many patients died on the table or soon afterwards. Operations inside the chest or abdomen were almost never attempted. Everything a modern hospital does in its operating theatres depends on a discovery that was made, and very nearly missed, in the 1840s.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The curious thing is that the means had been available for decades. The English chemist Humphry Davy experimented on himself with nitrous oxide around 1800, noticed that it relieved the pain of a toothache, and suggested in print that it might be used in surgery. Nobody acted on the idea. The gas instead became a fashionable entertainment. Because it made those who breathed it giddy and talkative, it was known as laughing gas, and travelling showmen charged audiences to watch volunteers stagger about the stage. Ether, a liquid known since the sixteenth century, was used in the same way at parties.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It was at one such show, in the American town of Hartford in 1844, that a dentist named Horace Wells noticed a volunteer gash his leg badly without seeming to feel it. The next day, Wells inhaled the gas himself and had a colleague pull out one of his teeth. He felt nothing. Eager to announce his discovery, he arranged a demonstration before the surgeons of Boston. It was a disaster. The bag of gas was withdrawn too early, the patient cried out, and the audience jeered. Wells was dismissed as a fraud and never recovered his reputation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Success went to his former partner, William Morton, who turned to ether after learning of its properties from a chemist. On 16 October 1846, at the Massachusetts General Hospital, Morton administered it to a young man while the hospital's senior surgeon removed a tumour from his neck. The patient lay still, and on waking said that he had felt no more than a scratching. The surgeon turned to the spectators and declared that what they had seen was no trick. News of the operation crossed the Atlantic by steamship, and within two months ether was being used in London and Paris.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The triumph was followed by an ugly quarrel. Morton tried to conceal the identity of his substance by adding colouring and scent, and applied for a patent, in the hope of charging a fee for every use. The medical profession was outraged, and since the smell of ether was unmistakable, the secret could not be kept. Wells, Morton and the chemist who had advised him then spent years disputing which of them deserved the credit and a reward from the government. None of them profited. Wells took his own life, Morton died in poverty, and the chemist ended his days in an asylum.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Ether had drawbacks. It irritated the lungs, caused vomiting and caught fire easily, a serious matter in rooms lit by gas or candles. In 1847 the Scottish doctor James Simpson, searching for something better, tested a series of chemicals by inhaling them with friends at his dining table. One evening they tried chloroform and woke up some time later on the floor. Chloroform was pleasanter and quicker than ether, and Simpson began giving it to women in childbirth. This met with opposition from some doctors and clergymen, who held that the pain of labour was natural or even divinely intended. The argument was largely settled in 1853, when Queen Victoria accepted chloroform for the birth of her eighth child and pronounced it delightful.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It took rather longer to discover that the new freedom from pain had not made surgery safe. Surgeons could now work slowly and carefully, and they undertook longer and more ambitious operations. But they still operated in their street clothes with unwashed hands and instruments, and more patients than ever died of infection in the days that followed. Only with the introduction of antiseptic methods by Joseph Lister in the 1860s, and later of sterile instruments and gowns, did the death rate begin to fall. Anaesthesia made modern surgery possible, but it needed a second revolution to make it survivable.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One mystery remains. More than a century and a half later, scientists still cannot fully explain how anaesthetics work. Substances with very different chemical structures all produce the same reversible loss of consciousness, and they do so not only in humans but in animals of every kind. The leading theories hold that the drugs interfere with particular proteins in the membranes of nerve cells, but the details are disputed. Every day, in hospitals around the world, millions of patients are safely rendered unconscious by a process that is still not completely understood.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Four kilometres beneath the surface of the central Pacific, between Hawaii and Mexico, lies a plain of soft mud larger than the continent of Europe. Scattered across it, half buried, are trillions of dark lumps the size of potatoes. They are known as polymetallic nodules, and they contain manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper in concentrations higher than in many mines on land. The metals are exactly those needed for the batteries of electric cars and for storing power from the wind and sun. A number of companies and governments are now preparing to collect them, and a fierce argument has broken out over whether they should be allowed to.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The nodules form by one of the slowest processes known to geology. Each begins with a small hard object, such as a fragment of shell or a shark's tooth. Metals dissolved in sea water settle on it layer by layer, at a rate of a few millimetres in a million years. A nodule that fits in the hand may have taken ten million years to grow. They were first hauled up by a British research ship in the 1870s, and in the 1970s several industrial groups built experimental machines to gather them, before a fall in metal prices put an end to the attempt.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The proposed method of mining is straightforward in principle. A vehicle the size of a combine harvester crawls across the sea bed, sucking up the top few centimetres of sediment along with the nodules. The nodules are separated and pumped up a pipe to a ship, and the leftover water and mud are discharged back into the sea. Supporters argue that this compares well with mining on land. No forests are cleared, no villages moved, and no waste rock heaped up. They point out that much of the world's cobalt comes from mines where conditions for workers are appalling, and that demand for these metals is expected to multiply as the world gives up oil.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Opponents do not deny the need for metals. Their case is that we know too little about what would be destroyed. The deep sea floor was long assumed to be almost lifeless. Expeditions to the Pacific plain have instead found thousands of species, the great majority of them new to science, including pale octopuses, glass sponges and worms of many kinds. Many of these animals live on the nodules themselves, which provide the only hard surface in an expanse of mud. Remove the nodules, and their habitat is gone for millions of years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is evidence about how slowly such a place recovers. In 1989, German scientists dragged a plough back and forth across a patch of sea bed off Peru to imitate the effect of mining. When researchers returned twenty-six years later, the tracks looked as fresh as if they had been made the day before, and the animals that feed by filtering the water had not come back. A further concern is the cloud of fine sediment that mining would stir up, both at the sea bed and where waste water is released. It could drift for hundreds of kilometres, smothering animals far beyond the mined area. In 2024, researchers also reported that the nodules appear to generate oxygen in complete darkness, a finding that is still disputed but which suggests how much remains unknown.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The legal position is unusual. The nodule fields lie in international waters, which belong to no country. Under a United Nations treaty, the mineral wealth of the sea bed there is declared to be the common heritage of mankind, and it is administered by a body based in Jamaica, the International Seabed Authority. The authority has issued more than thirty licences for exploration, but it has not yet agreed the rules under which commercial mining could begin. In 2021, the small Pacific island state of Nauru, acting as sponsor for a Canadian company, invoked a clause in the treaty that obliged the authority to complete its regulations within two years. The deadline passed without agreement, leaving the situation uncertain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, opposition has grown. More than thirty countries, among them France, Germany and the United Kingdom, have called for a pause or a ban until the consequences are better understood. Several large car makers and technology firms have promised not to buy metals from the deep sea. Others take the opposite view. Norway has voted to open part of its own waters to exploration, and some Pacific island nations see in the nodules a rare source of income.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The argument may yet be overtaken by events. Battery chemistry is changing quickly, and the newest designs use little or no cobalt or nickel. Recycling of old batteries is improving. If demand for the metals proves smaller than forecast, the commercial case for going to the bottom of the ocean could weaken of its own accord. For the moment, the question is whether humanity will, for once, examine an ecosystem before deciding to exploit it, and not afterwards.

passage.title: Is there a best age to learn a language?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is widely believed that children pick up languages effortlessly and that adults struggle. The belief has shaped educational policy in many countries, where the teaching of English or another foreign language now begins in the first years of primary school or even earlier. The scientific basis for it is an idea known as the critical period hypothesis. The evidence, examined closely, supports part of the popular belief and contradicts the rest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The hypothesis was set out in 1967 by the neurologist Eric Lenneberg. He observed that children who suffered damage to the language areas of the brain often recovered their speech completely, while adults with similar injuries rarely did, and he proposed that the brain has a special readiness for language that fades at about the age of puberty. The strongest support came from tragic cases of children who had been deprived of language altogether. A girl known as Genie, discovered in California in 1970 after being kept in isolation until the age of thirteen, eventually learned a good many words but never mastered grammar. It seems clear that a first language must be acquired in childhood if it is to be acquired fully.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whether the same applies to a second language is a different question, and a harder one to answer. The most ambitious attempt was published in 2018 by researchers who designed an online grammar quiz that attracted nearly seven hundred thousand people, two thirds of them speakers of English as a foreign language. By relating each person's score to the age at which they had started learning and the number of years they had studied, the team estimated how the ability to learn grammar changes over a lifetime. Their conclusion was that it remains high until about seventeen or eighteen, considerably later than Lenneberg had supposed, and then declines steadily. To reach the level of a native speaker, however, learners needed to have started by about the age of ten, simply because it takes many years of exposure to get there.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The study, like others before it, found no sudden cut-off. The decline with age is gradual, and it varies with the aspect of language concerned. Pronunciation is the most sensitive. People who begin a language after early childhood nearly always retain a detectable accent, however fluent they become. Vocabulary shows no such limit, and can be learned efficiently at any age.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If older learners are at a disadvantage in the long run, they have the advantage at the start. This has been demonstrated repeatedly. In a large project in Spain, pupils who began English at eleven were compared with pupils who had begun at eight, after each group had received the same number of hours of teaching. The late starters did better on almost every measure. Older children and adults have more developed memories, they can already read, they understand explanations of grammar, and they know how to study. Young children learn in a different way, by absorbing patterns from enormous quantities of speech, and a few lessons a week do not provide enough.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This finding has an awkward implication for schools. The policy of starting foreign languages ever earlier assumes that young children's natural gift will operate in the classroom. In practice, an hour or two a week from a teacher who may not be fluent bears little resemblance to the experience of a child growing up surrounded by a language. Studies in several European countries have found that pupils who started early were, by the end of secondary school, no better than those who started later, and sometimes less motivated, having spent years making little visible progress. Early teaching does appear to help in one respect, which is that children who meet a language young tend to have more positive attitudes towards foreign languages in general.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Researchers also question whether the decline in adult learning is purely a matter of biology. An immigrant child attends school in the new language, plays in it, and is corrected patiently for years. An immigrant adult often works among speakers of his or her own language, has little time to study, and is embarrassed to make mistakes. When adults do receive the kind of intensive exposure that children get, some of them attain very high levels indeed. The observed differences between ages reflect circumstances as well as brains.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: What practical conclusions follow? For parents, there is no need for alarm if a child has not begun a second language by the age of five. For schools, the quantity and quality of teaching matter more than the starting age, and a later, more intensive course may be a better use of limited resources than a thin layer spread over many years. And for adults who have always meant to learn, the news is better than they may have feared. They will probably never be mistaken for natives. In every other respect, there is no age at which it is too late to begin.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a desert plateau in southern Peru, between the Andes and the Pacific, the ground is marked with lines. Some run perfectly straight for kilometres, crossing dry riverbeds and climbing hills without deviating. Others form triangles, spirals and long narrow rectangles. And among them are about seventy figures of animals and plants, a hummingbird, a monkey with a coiled tail, a spider, a whale, each drawn with a single continuous line and some of them more than two hundred metres across. They were made by the Nazca people, who lived in the valleys nearby between about 100 BC and AD 700. From the ground they are almost impossible to make out. They became widely known only in the 1930s, when aircraft began to fly over the region.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: How they were made is the simplest part of the puzzle. The surface of the plateau is covered with small stones that have been darkened by long exposure to the air. Beneath them lies pale, yellowish soil. By clearing the stones aside, the makers exposed the lighter ground, and the contrast produced the line. The straight lines could have been laid out with nothing more than wooden stakes and cord, and the remains of such stakes have been found at the ends of some of them. For the figures, it is thought that a small drawing was enlarged section by section using a grid. Experiments have shown that a team of a dozen people could produce one of the large figures in a couple of days.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That they have survived is due to the climate. The plateau is one of the driest places on earth, receiving perhaps twenty minutes of light rain a year. There is little wind at ground level, because the dark stones heat up in the sun and create a cushion of warm air above the surface. With almost nothing to disturb them, marks made two thousand years ago remain sharp.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The difficult question is why they were made. The first scholar to study them in detail, the American historian Paul Kosok, was standing on one of the lines at sunset on the shortest day of the year when he noticed that it pointed directly at the setting sun. He concluded that the lines formed a vast astronomical calendar, used to fix the dates for planting and harvest. His work was continued for half a century by a German mathematician, Maria Reiche, who lived beside the lines, measured them, and campaigned for their protection. The theory has not stood up well. When an astronomer tested the directions of the lines by computer in the 1960s, he found that no more of them pointed to significant positions of the sun, moon or stars than would be expected by chance.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: More recent research has looked to the thing the Nazca needed most, which was water. Their valleys depended on rivers that flow from the mountains for only part of the year and sometimes fail entirely. Several studies have reported that many of the straight lines lead towards sources of water or trace the course of underground channels. Broken pottery, apparently smashed on purpose, has been found along the lines and at the points where they meet, together with shells brought from the coast, which in the Andes were a traditional offering in prayers for rain. The current view of most archaeologists is that the lines were paths, walked in procession during ceremonies intended to bring water, and that the act of making and walking them mattered more than how they looked.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The animal figures fit this interpretation less neatly, and they may have had a somewhat different purpose. Many of the creatures shown, such as the monkey and the hummingbird, do not live in the desert but in the rainforest on the far side of the mountains, and several are associated in Andean belief with water and fertility. As for the objection that the figures could not be seen by those who made them, it has been pointed out that they were perhaps not meant for human eyes at all, but for gods who looked down from the mountains or the sky.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One explanation can be set aside. A best-selling book of the 1960s proposed that the long cleared strips were runways for the spacecraft of visitors from another world. Apart from the absence of any evidence, the suggestion overlooks the fact that the ground is soft, and that anything landing on it would sink. Archaeologists have also objected that the idea is insulting, since it assumes that the ancient inhabitants of Peru were incapable of work that requires only patience and string.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Discoveries continue. Since 2018, a Japanese team using high-resolution aerial photographs and artificial intelligence trained to recognise faint patterns has identified several hundred previously unknown figures, most of them smaller and older than the famous ones and placed beside ancient footpaths, where travellers would have seen them. At the same time, the lines face new threats. A major highway cuts through them, illegal mining and squatters have encroached on the edges, and in 2014 activists laying out a banner beside the hummingbird left footprints that will last for centuries. A surface that preserves every mark for thousands of years preserves the careless ones too.
