passage.title: The desert that feeds a rainforest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Amazon rainforest and the Sahara desert could hardly be more different. One is the wettest and most densely living region on earth, the other among the driest and emptiest, and they are separated by the width of the Atlantic Ocean. Yet research over the past three decades has shown that they are connected. Every year, winds lift hundreds of millions of tonnes of dust from the surface of the Sahara and carry it westwards, and part of that dust falls on the Amazon, where it supplies the forest with something it cannot do without.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To understand why, one must begin with a paradox about tropical soil. The luxuriant growth of a rainforest suggests rich ground beneath it. In fact, Amazonian soils are among the poorest in the world. Heavy rain, falling for millions of years, has washed most of the soluble minerals out of them. The forest survives by recycling. When a leaf falls, fungi and insects break it down within weeks, and the roots of living trees, which spread in a dense mat just below the surface, absorb the nutrients almost before they reach the soil. Very little is stored in the ground. This is why land cleared of forest for farming so often becomes useless after a few harvests.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Even an efficient system leaks. Each year some nutrients are carried away by the rivers, and of these the most critical is phosphorus, which every living cell requires and which, unlike nitrogen, cannot be drawn from the air. If the losses were not made good, the forest would slowly starve. For a long time nobody knew where the replacement came from.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The answer began to emerge when scientists analysed the chemistry of dust collected in South America and matched it to a particular source. It is a depression in the country of Chad, on the southern edge of the Sahara, known as the Bodele. Thousands of years ago, when the climate of North Africa was wetter, the depression lay at the bottom of an enormous lake. As the lake dried, it left behind a thick layer of the remains of microscopic organisms that had lived in its waters, and these remains are rich in phosphorus. Today the Bodele is the dustiest place on the planet. The surrounding mountains funnel the wind across it at high speed, and on about a hundred days a year great plumes rise from its surface.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The scale of the transfer has been measured from space. Between 2007 and 2013, a satellite equipped with a laser recorded the quantity of dust in the air across the Atlantic at different heights. From these observations, a team in the United States calculated that on average about a hundred and eighty million tonnes of dust leave Africa each year, of which some twenty-eight million tonnes reach the Amazon basin. The phosphorus this contains amounts to about twenty-two thousand tonnes, which is roughly equal to the amount the forest loses each year to its rivers. The two figures, in other words, appear to balance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The quantity varies greatly from one year to the next, and the variation is linked to rainfall in the Sahel, the belt of dry grassland along the desert's southern margin. When the Sahel has a wet year, less dust crosses the ocean in the following year, perhaps because more vegetation holds the soil in place, or because rain washes the dust out of the air before it can travel far. This raises a question about the future. Some climate models predict that a warmer world will bring more rain to the Sahel. If so, the supply of dust could fall, with consequences for the forest that are difficult to foresee.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Amazon is not the only beneficiary. Much of the dust falls into the Atlantic on the way, where the iron it contains feeds the growth of plankton, the microscopic plants at the base of the ocean's food chain. Further north, Saharan dust builds up the soils of Caribbean islands, and it is thought to have supplied much of the red earth of Bermuda and the Bahamas. Nor is the influence wholly benign. Thick dust lowers the quality of the air in the Caribbean and the southern United States, and it has been blamed for outbreaks of asthma. It also has a curious effect on the weather. Dry, dusty air over the Atlantic tends to suppress the formation of hurricanes, so that seasons with heavy dust are often seasons with fewer storms.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The connection between the desert and the forest is a striking illustration of a principle that ecologists have come to appreciate, which is that no ecosystem is self-contained. A forest in Brazil depends on a dried lake bed in Chad that happens to lie in the path of the wind. It is also a reminder of how such links can go unnoticed. The dust has been crossing the ocean for thousands of years, and until instruments were placed in orbit, nobody could say how much there was.

passage.title: The spaces between home and work

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1989, the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg published a book with an unusually long subtitle, listing cafes, coffee shops, bookshops, bars and hair salons. His argument was that a healthy community needs places of a particular kind. Home, he said, is the first place in a person's life and work is the second. The third place is somewhere else, where people gather informally, regularly and by choice. The French have the cafe, the English the pub, the Italians the piazza. In the suburbs of post-war America, where houses were separated from shops by miles of road and almost every journey was made by car, such places had all but disappeared, and Oldenburg believed that social life had suffered as a result.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: He identified several features that true third places share. They stand on neutral ground, where nobody is host and nobody guest, and people may come and go as they please. They are levellers, in which a person's rank or wealth counts for little. The main activity is conversation. They are close to hand and open for long hours, so that a visit needs no planning. They have regulars, whose presence gives the place its character and who make newcomers feel that they have joined something. And they are plain. An establishment that is too smart makes people self-conscious and discourages them from lingering.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The value of such places, Oldenburg suggested, lies in the kind of relationships they make possible. At home and at work, we deal with people to whom we are bound by strong ties of family or duty. In a third place, we meet acquaintances whom we might not invite to our homes but are glad to see. Sociologists call these weak ties, and research has repeatedly shown that they matter more than might be expected. In a famous study of how people found jobs, most had heard of the vacancy not from close friends, who tend to know the same things we do, but from someone they saw only occasionally. More recently, psychologists have found that brief exchanges with people we barely know, such as the person who serves us coffee, make a measurable contribution to how happy we feel on a given day.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is a civic argument as well. A third place is one of the few settings in which people of different ages, occupations and opinions talk to one another without having chosen to. Oldenburg saw in this an informal school of democracy. Problems of the neighbourhood are aired, rumours are corrected, and those who disagree learn that their opponents are human.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The idea was taken up enthusiastically by business. The head of one very large chain of coffee shops adopted the phrase to describe what his company sold, which was not so much coffee as somewhere to sit. Oldenburg was unimpressed. A branch of a global chain, in which customers queue in silence, work alone at laptops with headphones on, and are encouraged to leave when they have finished, lacked almost everything he had described. The regulars do not know one another, and the staff are too busy to talk.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Critics have raised objections to the concept itself. Oldenburg's examples were places where men had traditionally gathered, and for much of history the tavern and the barber's shop were closed to women, who were expected to find their company at home. Access also depends on money. The price of a coffee is a small barrier to some people and a real one to others, and a cafe will not tolerate for long a customer who buys nothing. For this reason, some writers argue that the most valuable third places are those that charge no admission at all, such as public libraries, parks and playgrounds, and that their closure through cuts in public spending is more damaging than the loss of any cafe.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Whether the internet can provide third places has been much debated. Online forums and games do allow strangers to converse on equal terms, and for people who are isolated by illness, disability or distance, they can be a lifeline. But they differ in an important respect. Online, we choose whom we talk to with great precision and can leave at the first sign of disagreement. A physical third place obliges us to rub along with whoever happens to be there.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The question has taken on new urgency. Surveys in many countries report that people have fewer close friends than a generation ago and spend more time alone. Working from home has removed, for many, even the daily contact of the office. In response, a number of cities have begun to treat third places as a form of infrastructure, as worthy of public investment as roads or drains. One practical lesson has emerged from their experiments. Such places cannot simply be designed and installed. They grow where people are allowed to stay without a reason, and they are created less by architects than by those who use them.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: If we were to meet an intelligent being from another planet, it would presumably be the product of an evolutionary history entirely separate from our own. In one sense, we already have. The octopus and its relatives, the squid and the cuttlefish, are molluscs, more closely related to snails and oysters than to any animal with a backbone. The last ancestor that we share with them lived more than five hundred million years ago and was probably a small worm-like creature with, at most, a few simple light-sensitive spots. Everything that an octopus has in the way of a brain evolved independently of ours.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: And it has a great deal. A common octopus possesses about five hundred million nerve cells, a number comparable to that of a dog and far beyond that of any other animal without a backbone. Their arrangement, however, is utterly unlike a mammal's. Only about a third are in the head. The rest are distributed along the eight arms, each of which contains a thick cord of nerves and thousands of suckers that can taste as well as touch. The arms have considerable independence. An arm that has been cut off will continue for some time to reach for food and pass it towards where the mouth would be. Researchers describe the animal as having a central brain that issues general instructions and eight subsidiary ones that work out the details.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The evidence of what this nervous system can do is abundant. Octopuses in laboratories learn to find their way through mazes, to unscrew the lids of jars, and to tell apart shapes and patterns. They are notorious for escaping. There are well-attested accounts of animals leaving their tanks at night, crossing the floor to another tank, eating the fish in it, and returning before morning. One octopus in a New Zealand aquarium squeezed through a gap at the top of its enclosure, slid across the floor and disappeared down a drainpipe that led to the sea.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Many keepers are convinced that individual octopuses have distinct characters, some bold and some shy, and that they recognise particular people. In one experiment, two members of staff dressed identically visited a group of octopuses each day. One always fed the animals, and the other always touched them with a bristly stick. Within two weeks, the octopuses behaved quite differently towards each of them, approaching the first and squirting water at the second. They also appear to play. Octopuses given an empty plastic bottle have been seen to blow it with a jet of water towards the current from a pump and to catch it when it floats back, over and over again, for no evident reward.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In the wild, the most striking discovery has been of tool use. Off the coast of Indonesia, a species known as the veined octopus collects the halves of coconut shells that people have thrown into the sea. It stacks them, carries them beneath its body while walking awkwardly on stiffened arms, and later assembles them into a shelter. Since the shells are of no use while they are being carried, and in fact make the animal more vulnerable, this is taken as evidence that it is planning for a future need.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why should a mollusc have evolved such abilities? The favoured explanation begins with the loss of the shell. The ancestors of the octopus were protected by a hard casing, as snails are. At some point this was abandoned, which allowed the animal to move fast and to squeeze into crevices, but left a soft, nutritious body exposed to every predator in the sea. Survival came to depend on wits, on hiding, deceiving and hunting flexibly. The same pressure produced the animal's extraordinary skin, which can change colour and texture in a fraction of a second to match its surroundings.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This account has an interesting consequence. In mammals and birds, high intelligence is associated with long lives and with living in groups, where there is an advantage in remembering who did what to whom. The octopus has neither. Most species are solitary, and most live for only a year or two. The female lays a single batch of eggs, guards them without eating until they hatch, and then dies. Each generation must learn everything afresh, with no parent to teach it. That so much mental capacity should be invested in so brief a life remains a puzzle.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The question of what, if anything, an octopus experiences has moved from philosophy into law. In 2021, after a review of more than three hundred scientific studies, the British government accepted that octopuses, along with crabs and lobsters, are capable of feeling pain and included them in legislation on animal welfare. Proposals to farm octopuses for food on an industrial scale have met strong opposition on the same grounds. Whatever one concludes, the animal has changed the terms of an old debate. Minds, it turns out, have arisen on this planet more than once.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A violin made in the workshop of Antonio Stradivari, who worked in the Italian city of Cremona until his death in 1737, can sell for more than ten million dollars. About six hundred of his instruments survive, and the world's leading soloists compete for the chance to play them. For two centuries it has been taken for granted that they possess a quality of sound that no later maker has equalled, and a small industry of scientists and craftsmen has devoted itself to finding out why. Recently, a more awkward question has been asked, which is whether the superiority exists at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The attempts to explain the secret make a long list. An early favourite was the varnish, which was said to contain some lost ingredient. Chemical analysis has since shown it to be a fairly ordinary mixture of oil and resin, of a kind used by furniture makers of the period. Attention then turned to the wood. Stradivari worked during an unusually cold period in European history, when trees in the Alps grew slowly and laid down narrow, even rings, and it was proposed that this dense timber gave his instruments their resonance. Another theory holds that the wood was soaked in a solution of minerals to protect it against woodworm, and that this treatment altered its acoustic properties. Others point to the geometry, to the precise curve of the front and back plates and the shape of the sound holes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Each of these ideas has its supporters, and none has been shown to be decisive. Modern makers have at their disposal medical scanners that reveal the thickness of every part of an old instrument to a fraction of a millimetre, and they can produce copies that match the originals in every measurable dimension. If there is a secret, it is not for want of information that it remains one.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The more radical challenge has come from experiments on listeners and players. The difficulty with any comparison of violins is that those taking part usually know which instrument is which, and knowing that one is holding a priceless antique is likely to colour one's impression of it. In 2010, a team led by the French researcher Claudia Fritz set out to remove that knowledge. At an international violin competition in the American city of Indianapolis, twenty-one experienced players were invited to a hotel room and asked to try six instruments, three of them new and three old, including two by Stradivari. The lights were dimmed, the players wore welding goggles so that they could not see what they were holding, and a touch of perfume was applied to the chin rest of each violin to disguise the smell of old wood.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The result caused a sensation. Asked which instrument they would most like to take home, thirteen of the twenty-one chose a new one. The least popular of the six was a Stradivarius. And when the players were asked to say whether the instrument they were holding was old or new, their answers were no better than guesses.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Critics objected that a hotel room is not a concert hall, and that the test had been brief. The team therefore repeated it in Paris on a larger scale. Ten renowned soloists each spent more than an hour with twelve violins, six new and six old, first in a rehearsal room and then in a concert hall with three hundred seats, playing alone and with an orchestra. Again the players wore goggles. Six of the ten chose a new violin as their favourite. In a further study, audiences in halls in Paris and New York were asked to judge which of two instruments, played behind a screen, carried better to the back of the room. They consistently preferred the new ones, and they too were unable to tell which was which.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These findings have not been universally accepted. Some musicians argue that a great old instrument takes months to get to know, and that its particular strengths, a wider range of tone colours perhaps, would not show in an afternoon. Others point out that the new violins in the tests were made by the finest living craftsmen and selected with care, whereas an old instrument may not be in the best condition. It has also been observed that almost every old violin has been substantially altered since it left its maker's bench, fitted with a longer neck and stronger internal parts to produce the louder sound that large modern halls demand. What we hear today is not quite what Stradivari made.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: None of this diminishes his achievement. He established the form of the instrument so successfully that makers have copied it for three hundred years, and the best of them are judged by how close they come. But the experiments suggest that part of what listeners hear in a Stradivarius is its reputation. Expectation shapes perception, in music as in the tasting of wine, and a belief repeated for long enough can come to feel like the evidence of the senses.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Bread, cheese, yoghurt, wine, beer, soy sauce, vinegar, chocolate and coffee have something in common. All of them owe their character to the activity of microbes. Fermentation, the process by which yeasts and bacteria transform the sugars in food, is among the oldest technologies that human beings possess, and it was practised for thousands of years by people who had no idea that microbes existed. It has recently returned to fashion, promoted for its supposed benefits to health. The history is remarkable enough without exaggeration.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The origins are lost, but they were almost certainly accidental. Fruit left in a container ferments by itself, since wild yeasts live on its skin, and grain that has got wet and begun to sprout will do the same. Chemical traces of a fermented drink made from rice, honey and fruit have been identified on fragments of pottery from a Chinese village nine thousand years old. Some archaeologists have gone further and proposed that the desire for beer, and not for bread, was what first persuaded hunters and gatherers in the Middle East to settle and cultivate cereals. The suggestion is impossible to prove, but large stone vessels apparently used for brewing have been found at a site in Turkey that is older than any known farm.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Whatever its beginnings, fermentation spread because it solved a practical problem, which was how to keep food from spoiling. Milk turns sour within a day in a warm climate. Made into cheese, it will last for months or years. Cabbage salted and packed into a barrel becomes sauerkraut, and remains edible through the winter. The principle is the same in each case. The harmless bacteria that carry out the fermentation produce acid or alcohol as a by-product, and in doing so create conditions in which the organisms that cause decay and disease cannot survive. In effect, people learned to defend their food by encouraging one group of microbes to drive out the rest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There were other advantages, less obvious to those who benefited from them. Fermentation can make food more nourishing. The process that turns soya beans into tempeh, in Indonesia, breaks down substances in the raw bean that interfere with digestion. Milk is a striking case. Most adults in the world cannot easily digest the sugar it contains, but in yoghurt and aged cheese much of that sugar has already been consumed by bacteria. Fermentation also removes poisons. Cassava, a root that is the staple food of several hundred million people in the tropics, contains compounds that release cyanide, and it must be soaked and fermented before it is safe to eat.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For most of history, the process was a mystery. Brewers knew that the froth from one batch would start the next, without knowing what the froth was. In the 1850s, the French chemist Louis Pasteur was asked by a manufacturer of alcohol from beetroot to find out why some of his vats were turning sour. Looking through a microscope, Pasteur saw that the healthy vats contained round yeast cells, while the spoiled ones swarmed with smaller, rod-shaped organisms. He concluded that fermentation was not a purely chemical reaction, as the leading scientists of the day maintained, but the work of living things, and that different organisms produced different results. The insight led directly to his later work on infectious disease.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Industrialisation changed the practice profoundly. Where bakers and brewers had relied on whatever mixture of microbes lived in their premises, manufacturers now used pure strains grown in laboratories, which gave a consistent product every time. Refrigeration and canning took over the task of preservation. Many traditional fermented foods were replaced by quicker imitations. Most supermarket pickles, for instance, are simply vegetables in vinegar, and much commercial bread is raised in an hour or two, where a traditional loaf took a day.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The current revival is driven largely by interest in the bacteria that inhabit the human gut. Fermented foods that have not been heated after fermentation contain large numbers of live microbes, and enthusiasts claim that eating them improves digestion, immunity and even mood. The evidence is mixed. A study at Stanford University in 2021 found that volunteers who ate several servings of fermented foods a day for ten weeks had a greater variety of bacteria in their gut and lower levels of certain markers of inflammation. That is encouraging, but it was a small study, and whether such changes lead to better health in the long run has not been shown. Most of the microbes in fermented foods do not settle permanently in the gut. They pass through.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, fermentation in a broader sense has become one of the most important industrial processes in the world. The citric acid in soft drinks, many vitamins, and antibiotics such as penicillin are produced by microbes grown in steel tanks. Since the 1980s, bacteria and yeasts have been genetically altered to manufacture substances they would never make in nature, including the insulin used by people with diabetes, which was formerly extracted from the organs of pigs. The technology of the brewer's vat, discovered by accident before history began, now produces a large share of the world's medicines.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Walk into the headquarters of almost any large company today and you will find the same arrangement. Rows of desks stretch across a floor without partitions, and managers sit among their staff. The open-plan office has become so universal that it is hard to remember it was once a radical experiment. Its promoters promised that it would transform the way people work together. The evidence that has accumulated over half a century suggests that it has done so, though not in the way they intended.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The idea was born in Germany in the late 1950s, when two brothers who ran a consultancy near Hamburg proposed what they called the office landscape. They believed that the traditional layout, with clerks in rows and executives behind closed doors, obstructed the flow of information. In their design, desks were grouped in irregular clusters according to who needed to talk to whom, separated by plants and curved screens, and nobody had a private room. The intention was democratic as well as practical.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The concept crossed the Atlantic and was soon altered. In 1964, an American designer, Robert Propst, introduced a system of movable panels and work surfaces that could be arranged to give each employee a semi-enclosed space, with room to spread out papers and to stand as well as sit. He intended it to be flexible and humane. Companies discovered that the panels could be used to pack the largest possible number of people into a floor, each in an identical box. The cubicle, as it became known, was born, and Propst spent his later years lamenting what had been done with his invention.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In the 1990s and 2000s, technology firms in California led a reaction against the cubicle, tearing down the panels and returning to open floors, now with bright colours, sofas and table football. The stated reason was collaboration. Chance meetings, it was argued, spark ideas, and walls prevent them. A less publicised reason was cost. An open floor holds far more desks than one divided into rooms, and property is among the largest expenses of any business in a city.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The complaints of those who work in such offices have been documented in survey after survey. The most frequent concerns noise, and in particular other people's conversations. Experiments show that background speech is far more disruptive than mechanical noise of the same volume, because the brain cannot help trying to follow it. After an interruption, it can take many minutes to regain full concentration on a demanding task. Lack of privacy comes next. People who feel that they are constantly observed report higher stress, and studies in Scandinavia have found that employees in open offices take more days of sick leave than those with rooms of their own, a difference attributed partly to the spread of infections and partly to strain.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These drawbacks might be worth bearing if the promised collaboration materialised. The most rigorous test of that claim was published in 2018 by two researchers at Harvard. They studied two large companies that were about to move staff from cubicles to fully open floors. For several weeks before and after the change, volunteers wore electronic badges that recorded, by means of sensors, when they were in conversation with a colleague, and the researchers also counted their emails and instant messages. The outcome was the opposite of what the companies had hoped. Face-to-face interaction fell by about seventy per cent, while electronic messages increased. Exposed to view on every side, people had put on headphones, avoided eye contact and typed to colleagues sitting a few metres away.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The researchers' explanation was that human beings need some control over their encounters. When a boundary is removed, they construct another, and a fourth wall, as they called it, of polite indifference is harder to penetrate than a door that can be knocked on. Later studies have refined the picture. Small open offices shared by a team of five or six seem to work reasonably well. It is the very large, undivided floor that produces withdrawal.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Designers have responded with a compromise that goes by various names. Staff are offered a range of settings, quiet rooms for concentrated work, booths for telephone calls, tables for meetings and open areas for casual conversation, and move between them as their tasks require. Often no one has a desk of their own. Whether this is an improvement or merely a further saving on space is disputed, and many employees dislike beginning each day by hunting for somewhere to sit. The spread of working from home has changed the question once again. If people can concentrate better in their own kitchens, the purpose of the office may come to be precisely the conversation that the open plan was supposed to encourage, and failed to.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most lakes are short-lived features of the landscape. They form in hollows left by glaciers or in the bends of rivers, and within ten or twenty thousand years they fill with sediment and vanish. Lake Baikal, in the south of Siberia, is a spectacular exception. It is at least twenty-five million years old, and it is still growing. It is also the deepest lake in the world, reaching more than sixteen hundred metres, and although several lakes cover a larger area, none holds more water. Baikal contains about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the surface of the planet, more than the five Great Lakes of North America combined.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The explanation for its age and depth lies in its origin. Baikal occupies a rift, a place where the crust of the earth is being pulled apart. The two sides are separating by a few millimetres a year, and the floor between them is sinking. Beneath the water lies a layer of sediment as much as seven kilometres thick, which has accumulated without interruption since the lake began. For geologists, a core drilled from this mud is an archive of the climate of central Asia over millions of years.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A lake so old has had time to evolve a fauna of its own. Of the two and a half thousand or so species of animal recorded in Baikal, around two thirds are found nowhere else. They include more than three hundred kinds of small shrimp-like creatures, some of them brightly coloured and as long as a finger, which between them consume much of the dead matter that falls to the bottom. There is a fish, the golomyanka, that has no scales, is nearly transparent, and gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs. A third of its body weight is oil, and when one is washed ashore and left in the sun, it is said to melt away, leaving only bones.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most famous inhabitant is the Baikal seal, the only species of seal in the world that lives exclusively in fresh water. How its ancestors arrived, several thousand kilometres from the nearest ocean, has long been debated. The most probable route is from the Arctic, up the rivers that drain northwards, at a time during the ice ages when ice sheets blocked those rivers and created great lakes along their course.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Baikal is renowned for the clarity of its water. In early summer, an object can be seen at a depth of forty metres. This is largely the work of a single animal, a tiny crustacean no bigger than a grain of rice, which is present in enormous numbers and filters bacteria and algae from the water. It is exquisitely adapted to cold and cannot survive in water much warmer than fifteen degrees. Another unusual feature is that the lake is rich in oxygen all the way to the bottom. In most deep lakes the lower layers are stagnant, but in Baikal cold surface water sinks each spring and autumn and carries oxygen down with it, so that animals live at every depth.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: For five months of the year, the lake is frozen. The ice may be more than a metre thick, strong enough to carry lorries, and so clear in places that it is possible to look down through it into the water. In the winter of 1904, during a war with Japan, the Russian army laid a railway track across the frozen surface in order to move troops eastwards, since the line around the southern shore had not yet been completed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The lake's isolation protected it for most of its history, but it now faces several threats. For nearly half a century, a mill on the southern shore that produced paper pulp discharged its waste into the water. It was finally closed in 2013, though millions of tonnes of toxic sludge remain in ponds beside the lake. Sewage from growing towns and from tourist developments has encouraged blankets of green algae along parts of the shore, an alarming sight in a lake famous for its purity, and in the same areas large numbers of the sponges that grow on the lake bed have died. The river that supplies half of Baikal's water flows in from Mongolia, where plans to build hydroelectric dams have caused concern.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The gravest threat may be the one that is hardest to address. The region around Baikal is warming considerably faster than the world as a whole. The period of ice cover has shortened by about two weeks over the past century, and the surface water in summer is measurably warmer. Many of the lake's unique species, like the little crustacean that keeps the water clear, have evolved over millions of years in constant cold. Animals that have never had to adapt to change may be poorly equipped to do so, and those that cannot have nowhere else to go.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It is difficult to think of a symbol that looks less impressive than a small empty circle. Yet the invention of zero has been called one of the greatest achievements of the human mind, and for most of history most civilisations managed without it. The Greeks, who laid the foundations of geometry, had no zero. Nor did the Romans, whose numerals are still used on clock faces and at the end of films. The idea arrived in Europe only in the Middle Ages, and when it did, it was met in some quarters with hostility.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To see why zero matters, it helps to distinguish two of its roles. The first is as a placeholder. In our system of writing numbers, the value of a digit depends on its position. The 2 in 25 means twenty, and the 2 in 250 means two hundred. For such a system to work, there must be a way of showing that a position is empty, so that 205 can be told apart from 25. The second role is as a number in its own right, a quantity that can be added, subtracted and multiplied like any other. The first idea occurred to several peoples independently. The second was far rarer.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The Babylonians of ancient Iraq used a positional system based on sixty, traces of which survive in our minutes and seconds. For many centuries they simply left a gap where a position was empty, which led to obvious confusion, and by about 300 BC their scribes had begun to insert a pair of slanted wedges as a marker. They never used it at the end of a number, however, and never treated it as a quantity. On the other side of the world, the Maya of Central America devised a symbol for zero, often drawn as a shell, for use in their elaborate calendar. It appears to have had no influence beyond their own culture.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The decisive step was taken in India. A dot used as a placeholder appears in an Indian manuscript on birch bark, parts of which have been dated to as early as the third or fourth century. And in the year 628, the astronomer Brahmagupta wrote a treatise in which, for the first time that we know of, zero is discussed as a number. He set out rules for calculating with it. A number minus itself is zero. A number plus zero is unchanged. A number multiplied by zero is zero. He also dealt with what we would call negative numbers, which he described as debts, in contrast to fortunes. On division by zero he was less successful, and the question was to trouble mathematicians for another thousand years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: From India the system travelled west. In the ninth century, the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote a book explaining the Indian method of calculation. The Arabic word for the empty place, sifr, is the origin of both the English words zero and cipher, and the Latin form of al-Khwarizmi's own name has given us the word algorithm. The numerals reached Europe by way of Spain and Italy. Their most effective champion was Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, the son of a merchant, who had learned the system as a boy in North Africa. In a book published in 1202, he showed how much faster and more reliable it made the keeping of accounts than the Roman numerals and counting boards then in use.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Adoption was slow nonetheless. In 1299, the city of Florence forbade bankers to use the new numerals in their records. The objection was not superstition, as is sometimes said, but fear of fraud. A zero could easily be turned into a six or a nine with a stroke of the pen, or added to the end of a figure to multiply it by ten, whereas Roman numerals were harder to alter. Merchants went on using the numerals privately, since they were so much more convenient, and with the spread of printing in the fifteenth century, which fixed the shapes of the digits, resistance faded.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There was an intellectual obstacle as well. The philosophy inherited from Aristotle held that nothingness could not exist, and a symbol for nothing seemed to some scholars to be a contradiction. Yet it was precisely the willingness to calculate with zero, and with quantities approaching it, that opened the way to the mathematics of the seventeenth century. The calculus developed by Newton and Leibniz depends on reasoning about what happens as a quantity becomes vanishingly small. Without it there would be no modern physics or engineering.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The latest chapter is the most familiar. Every digital computer represents information as a pattern of two states, written as one and zero. Each photograph, song and message stored on a phone is, at bottom, an immense string of those two digits. A concept that entire civilisations did without, and that others regarded with suspicion, has become half of the alphabet in which the modern world is written.

passage.title: Saving power for a windless night

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The cost of electricity from wind turbines and solar panels has fallen so far that in much of the world it is now cheaper than power from coal or gas. One awkward fact stands in the way of relying on it. The wind does not always blow, the sun sets every evening, and people want electricity at times that have nothing to do with either. An electricity grid must match supply and demand second by second. As the share of wind and solar power grows, the ability to store energy when it is plentiful and release it when it is scarce becomes the central problem of the whole system.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much the oldest and largest form of storage has nothing to do with batteries. In a pumped hydroelectric scheme, two reservoirs are built at different heights. When electricity is abundant and cheap, it is used to pump water uphill. When it is needed, the water is allowed to run back down through turbines. The first such plants were built in the Alps in the 1890s, and the method still accounts for the great majority of the world's storage capacity. About three quarters of the energy put in is recovered, and a large plant can deliver power for many hours. The limitation is geography. A scheme requires mountains, a great deal of water and the flooding of a valley, and in many countries the best sites have already been used.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The fastest-growing technology is the lithium-ion battery, the same kind that powers phones and electric cars. Mass production for vehicles has cut its cost by about nine tenths in a decade, and installations the size of several football pitches, containing thousands of battery units in steel containers, are now connected to grids in Australia, California and China. Their great strength is speed. A battery can respond to a change in demand within a fraction of a second, far faster than any power station. Their weakness is duration. Most are designed to discharge for between two and four hours, which is enough to carry solar power from the afternoon into the evening but not to cover several still, cloudy days in winter.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: For longer periods, engineers are exploring a range of alternatives. In a flow battery, energy is held in two tanks of liquid, which are pumped past each other across a membrane. To store more, one simply builds bigger tanks, and the liquids do not wear out as the materials of a solid battery do. Another approach compresses air into underground caverns left by salt mining and releases it through a turbine. A plant of this kind has operated in Germany since 1978. More recent ideas use surplus electricity to heat sand or molten salt to several hundred degrees in insulated silos, or to raise and lower enormous weights.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The hardest case is storage between seasons. In northern countries, solar panels produce most in summer, while demand peaks in winter. No battery could economically hold energy for six months. The leading candidate for this task is hydrogen, which can be made by using electricity to split water, kept in tanks or underground, and later burned in a turbine or passed through a fuel cell. The drawback is waste. By the time the electricity has been turned into hydrogen and back again, only about a third of the original energy remains. Supporters argue that this matters less than it seems if the electricity used would otherwise have been thrown away, as increasingly happens when wind farms are switched off because the grid cannot absorb their output.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some of the most promising storage is not on the grid at all. An electric car spends more than nine tenths of its life parked, with a battery far larger than a household needs in a day. With suitable equipment, cars could charge when power is plentiful and feed a little back at the evening peak. Trials in several countries have shown that the technology works. Whether owners will accept it, given concerns about wear on the battery, is another matter. A simpler step is to shift demand instead of supply. Water heaters, freezers and car chargers can be programmed to run when electricity is abundant, which reduces the amount of storage required in the first place.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Storage also has costs beyond money. Lithium, cobalt and nickel must be mined, often in places where environmental rules are weak, and the extraction of lithium from salt flats in South America consumes large quantities of water in very dry regions. Recycling of batteries is technically possible but still on a small scale. Researchers are developing batteries based on sodium, which can be obtained from ordinary salt and is available everywhere, though at present they are heavier for the energy they hold, a disadvantage that matters little for a battery that sits in a field.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: No single technology is likely to prevail. The requirement is for a mixture, fast batteries to steady the grid from second to second, pumped water and other methods to shift energy across a day or a week, and perhaps hydrogen for the longest gaps, together with stronger cables to carry power from where the weather is favourable to where it is not. The engineering is largely understood. What remains uncertain is how quickly it can be built, and who will pay.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Cut through the trunk of a tree that has grown in a climate with seasons, and you will see a pattern of concentric rings. Each ring represents a year. In spring, when growth is rapid, the tree lays down large, thin-walled cells that appear pale. As the summer advances, the cells become smaller and denser, forming a darker band, and in winter growth stops altogether. The sharp boundary between one year's dark wood and the next year's pale wood marks the turn of the year. That the rings can be counted to find a tree's age has been known since ancient times. That they can be read as a detailed record of the past was the discovery of an American astronomer.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Andrew Douglass was working at an observatory in Arizona in the early 1900s, studying the cycle of spots on the sun. He wondered whether the cycle affected the weather on earth and looked for a long record of climate with which to test the idea. It occurred to him that trees might provide one. In the dry south-west, a tree grows a wide ring in a wet year and a narrow one in a drought, and since all the trees in a district experience the same weather, they all show the same sequence of wide and narrow rings. He never did establish a clear link with sunspots. What he had found instead was a method of dating.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The principle is known as cross-dating. The sequence of ring widths over several decades is as distinctive as a bar code. If the pattern in the outer rings of an old beam matches the pattern in the inner rings of a living tree whose dates are known, the two can be overlapped, and the calendar is extended back to the year in which the older tree began to grow. By joining together timbers of different ages in this way, researchers have built continuous sequences reaching back thousands of years. The longest, assembled from oaks preserved in the bogs and river gravels of central Europe, covers more than twelve thousand years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Douglass applied the method to a question that had long puzzled archaeologists, the age of the abandoned stone villages of the American south-west. Nobody knew whether they were five hundred or five thousand years old. By 1929 he had a sequence from living trees running back to about 1300, and a separate, floating sequence made from roof beams taken from the ruins, of unknown date. That summer, a charred log dug from a site in Arizona supplied the missing section and joined the two. At a stroke, some forty settlements could be assigned dates accurate to the year.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The technique has since been put to a remarkable variety of uses. Historians have dated the timbers of cathedrals, ships and paintings on wooden panels, sometimes exposing forgeries. Because a precise date can be attached to each ring, wood of known age was used to check, and then to correct, the method of radiocarbon dating, which had been giving results that were too young by several centuries for the most ancient samples. Tree rings also record events. A fire leaves a scar that is later grown over. A year of intense cold may damage the cells and produce a so-called frost ring. A sequence of very narrow rings in trees across the northern hemisphere, beginning in the year 536, bears witness to a catastrophe, now attributed to massive volcanic eruptions, that dimmed the sun and caused harvests to fail from Ireland to China.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The oldest individual trees are not, as might be supposed, the giants of the forest. They are the bristlecone pines of the White Mountains in California, small twisted trees that grow at an altitude of three thousand metres in poor soil and bitter cold. Some are more than four and a half thousand years old. Their slow growth produces wood so dense and so full of resin that it resists insects and decay, and dead trunks lie on the ground for thousands of years, allowing the record to be pushed back further still.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It is rarely necessary to fell a tree to read it. A hollow drill, turned by hand, removes a core no thicker than a pencil from the bark to the centre, and the tree heals the wound. One notorious exception occurred in 1964, when a student researcher, whose drill had become stuck in a bristlecone pine in Nevada, was given permission to cut the tree down to recover it. When the rings were counted, the tree proved to have been nearly five thousand years old, and the oldest then known.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Today the main use of tree rings is in the study of climate. Reliable measurements of temperature made with instruments go back little more than a century and a half. Rings allow that record to be extended over one or two thousand years, so that the warming of recent decades can be set against the natural variation of the past. The method has its difficulties. Growth responds to rainfall and to the age of the tree as well as to temperature, and separating these influences requires careful statistics. But combined with evidence from ice cores, corals and lake sediments, tree rings have shown that the present rate of warming has no parallel in the period they cover.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A visitor walking through the galleries of a large museum might reasonably suppose that he or she is looking at the collection. In fact, what is on show is a tiny fraction of it. The Natural History Museum in London holds some eighty million specimens and displays far fewer than one in a hundred. The great art museums typically exhibit between two and five per cent of what they own. The rest is kept in basements, in warehouses on the edge of the city, and increasingly in purpose-built stores many miles away. To some critics this seems a scandal, a hoard of treasures locked away from the public that paid for them. People who work in museums see it differently.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: There are practical reasons why much cannot be shown. Many objects are too fragile. Watercolours, textiles, photographs and manuscripts fade irreversibly in light, and the usual rule is that such an item may be displayed for a few months and must then rest in darkness for several years. Others are of interest only to specialists, such as the ten thousand broken pieces of pottery from an excavation, each recorded and numbered, which taken together tell an archaeologist a great deal and which no visitor would wish to look at.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In museums of natural history, the stored material is not a reserve for the galleries at all. It is the reason the institution exists. A drawer containing three hundred examples of the same species of beetle, collected in different places over two centuries, is a scientific instrument. By comparing them, a researcher can see how the insect varies, how its range has shifted and when it disappeared from a particular region. The specimen on which the first description of a species was based has a special status, and is kept permanently so that any later doubt about the identity of the species can be settled by returning to it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The value of such collections has grown with the techniques available for studying them. The collectors of the nineteenth century could not have imagined that DNA would one day be extracted from the skins of birds they had shot, or that the chemistry of a feather would reveal what the bird had been eating. Eggshells gathered by naturalists before 1940 provided the evidence, decades later, that the pesticide DDT was causing the shells of birds of prey to become thinner. Plants pressed and dried two hundred years ago are being used to measure how the timing of flowering has changed as the climate has warmed. No one can say what questions will be asked of the collections in another century, which is the strongest argument for keeping them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Storage is nevertheless a heavy burden. Rooms must be held at a steady temperature and humidity. Insects that eat wool, fur and feathers have to be kept at bay, formerly with poisons and now more often by freezing anything that enters the building. Every object needs a record, and in older institutions large parts of the collection have never been properly catalogued, so that curators do not know exactly what they have. Thefts have come to light years after the event because nobody had noticed that the items were missing.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: This raises the question of whether museums should ever dispose of things. In many countries the idea is close to taboo. Donors give objects in the belief that they will be kept for ever, and a museum that sold a painting to pay for repairs to its roof would find future gifts drying up. Professional codes generally permit disposal only when an object is a duplicate, damaged beyond use, or outside the museum's field, and require that it be offered first to another public collection. Those in favour of a looser approach point out that collections cannot grow indefinitely, and that an object lying unseen and unstudied in one museum might be the centrepiece of another.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A different response is to open the stores themselves. A number of museums have built storage facilities that visitors can enter, walking between glass-fronted racks while conservators work in view. In Rotterdam, a museum of art has constructed a building shaped like a bowl and covered in mirrors, in which its entire holdings of more than a hundred and fifty thousand works are kept on shelves and sliding screens that the public can tour. Supporters say that this makes plain how a museum actually operates. Sceptics reply that looking at racks of unlabelled objects through glass is not the same as understanding them.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The most far-reaching change is digital. Museums are photographing their collections and publishing the images and records online, where anyone may search them. A specialist in Brazil can now examine a beetle held in Berlin without leaving her desk, and several institutions have invited volunteers to help by transcribing the handwritten labels on millions of specimens. The work is slow and costly, and only a small proportion has been done. But it holds out the prospect that the hidden nine tenths will, for the first time, be visible to all.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1729, a French astronomer named Jean-Jacques de Mairan performed an experiment on a plant. He had noticed that the leaves of a mimosa open towards the sun each morning and fold at dusk, and he wondered what would happen if the plant were deprived of light. He shut one in a dark cupboard and found that, for several days, the leaves went on opening and closing at the usual times. The plant, it appeared, did not simply respond to the sun. It carried a clock of its own.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: We now know that almost every living thing does the same, from bacteria to human beings. These internal rhythms are called circadian, from the Latin for about a day, and the name is exact. People who volunteer to live for weeks in caves or windowless rooms, without any clue to the time, continue to sleep and wake in a regular cycle, but it drifts. For most, the natural period is slightly longer than twenty-four hours. In ordinary life, the clock is corrected each day by light, and above all by the light of morning.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The machinery was worked out in the late twentieth century, largely through experiments on fruit flies, and it earned three American scientists a Nobel Prize in 2017. Inside each cell, certain genes direct the production of proteins which gradually build up, and which, on reaching a high enough level, switch off the genes that made them. The proteins then decay, the genes switch on again, and the cycle repeats, taking about a day to complete. In mammals, the countless clocks in the cells of the body are kept in step by a cluster of some twenty thousand nerve cells at the base of the brain, directly above the point where the nerves from the eyes cross.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The clock governs far more than sleep. Body temperature falls to its lowest in the hours before dawn and peaks in the early evening. Blood pressure rises sharply on waking. The hormone that prepares the body for sleep is released as darkness falls, and the liver, the gut and the immune system all follow daily schedules. One consequence is that the time at which a medicine is taken can alter its effect, and trials have shown that some drugs for cancer and for blood pressure work better, or do less harm, at particular hours.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, the clock and the day were in agreement. Artificial light has changed that. The signal that resets the clock is carried by special cells in the eye that are most sensitive to blue light, of the kind that is abundant in daylight and also in the glow of screens and modern lamps. Bright light in the evening tells the brain that it is still day, delays the release of the sleep hormone and pushes the whole cycle later. At the same time, people who spend their days indoors receive far less morning light than their ancestors did. The result is a clock that runs late and is only weakly set.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The people most severely affected are those who work at night. About one worker in five in industrial countries does some form of shift work. Their clocks rarely adapt fully, since on days off they return to a daytime routine, and they are obliged to be alert when their bodies are prepared for sleep and to sleep when they are prepared for activity. Large studies of nurses and factory workers have linked long periods of night work with higher rates of diabetes, heart disease and some cancers, and accidents at work and on the road are more frequent in the early hours.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A milder version of the same conflict affects a much larger group. People differ in their natural timing. Some are early types, alert at dawn, and others late types, who come to life in the evening. The tendency is partly inherited, and it shifts with age, reaching its latest point at around nineteen or twenty. Teenagers who cannot fall asleep before midnight and cannot wake for school are not being lazy. Their clocks have moved. Late types forced to rise early on working days and sleeping late at weekends live in a state that researchers have named social jet lag, as if they flew across several time zones every Friday and back every Monday. A number of schools that have experimented with a later start to the day have reported better attendance and improved results.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The practical advice that follows from all this is simple, though not always easy to act on. Seek daylight early in the day, preferably outdoors. Keep lights low and screens dim in the last hours of the evening. Go to bed and get up at roughly the same times, including at weekends. And for those who design timetables for schools, hospitals and factories, there is a larger lesson. The human body is not a machine that performs equally at any hour, and arrangements that ignore its rhythms carry a cost.
